query: What do recent (2023-2026) reviews, perspectives and roadmap papers identify as the OPEN PROBLEMS and FUTURE DIRECTIONS for self-driving laboratories, specifically in materials chemistry and electrochemistry? Give DOIs. I want the concrete, named challenges rather than generalities: orchestration/interoperability standards (SiLA2, LabOP, AnIML, Bluesky, Chemputer/chi), FAIR data and metadata capture, reproducibility and round-robin benchmarking between labs, the shortage of negative results, closing the loop with multiple ORTHOGONAL characterization modalities rather than a single scalar objective, multi-fidelity and multi-objective optimization, transfer/meta-learning across chemistries, human-in-the-loop and error recovery, and cost/accessibility. Which of these are described as still unsolved as of 2026?

Decompose the input task into a set of sub-objectives that need to
be met in order to form the answer. Subsequently, when working on solving
the query, you can focus on these objectives one by one. Note that the

info.name: clinical_trials_search

Search for clinical trials, with support for repeated calls and concurrent execution.

query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'
        >>> 'AREA[Phase]PHASE3'

    Location Search:
        Use SEARCH operator for compound location queries:
        >>> 'cancer AND SEARCH[Location](AREA[LocationCity]Boston AND AREA[LocationState]Massachusetts)'

    Complex Boolean:
        Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses:
        >>> '(cancer OR tumor) AND NOT (EXPANSION[None]pediatric OR AREA[StdAge]CHILD)'

    Date Ranges:
        Use RANGE to specify date ranges with formats like "yyyy-MM" or "yyyy-MM-dd".
        Note that MIN and MAX can be used for open-ended ranges:
        >>> AREA[ResultsFirstPostDate]RANGE[2015-01-01, MAX]

Operators:
    EXPANSION[type]: Controls term expansion
        - None: Exact match only, case and accent sensitive
        - Term: Includes lexical variants (plurals, spellings)
        - Concept: Includes UMLS synonyms
        - Relaxation: Relaxes adjacency requirements (default)
        - Lossy: Allows missing partial terms

    COVERAGE[type]: Controls text matching
        - FullMatch: Must match entire field
        - StartsWith: Must match beginning of field
        - EndsWith: Must match end of field
        - Contains: Must match part of field (default)

    AREA[field]: Specifies field to search
        - See Field Reference for available fields

    SEARCH[type]: Groups field searches
        - Location: Groups location-related fields
        - Study: Groups study-related fields

Usage Notes:
    - All search expressions are implicitly OR expressions
    - Operator precedence (highest to lowest): terms/source operators, NOT/context operators, AND, OR
    - Use quotes for exact phrase matching: "heart attack"
    - Use parentheses for grouping: (heart OR cardiac) AND attack
    - Use backslash to escape operators: \AND
    - Default expansion is EXPANSION[Relaxation]
    - Default coverage is COVERAGE[Contains]

Field Reference:
    High Priority Fields (weight >= 0.8):
        - NCTId (1.0): Trial identifier
        - Acronym (1.0): Study acronym
        - BriefTitle (0.89): Short title
        - OfficialTitle (0.85): Full official title
        - Condition (0.81): Medical condition
        - InterventionName (0.8): Primary intervention name
        - OverallStatus: Trial status

    Medium Priority Fields (0.5-0.79):
        - InterventionOtherName (0.75): Alternative intervention names
        - Phase (0.65): Trial phase
        - StdAge (0.65): Standard age groups
        - Keyword (0.6): Study keywords
        - BriefSummary (0.6): Short description
        - SecondaryOutcomeMeasure (0.5): Secondary outcomes

    Low Priority Fields (< 0.5):
        - DesignPrimaryPurpose (0.3): Primary purpose of study
        - StudyType (0.3)
        - Various descriptive, location, and administrative fields

Supported Enums:
    Phase:
        - EARLY_PHASE1: Early Phase 1
        - PHASE1: Phase 1
        - PHASE2: Phase 2
        - PHASE3: Phase 3
        - PHASE4: Phase 4
        - NA: Not Applicable

    StandardAge:
        - CHILD: Child
        - ADULT: Adult
        - OLDER_ADULT: Older Adult

    Status:
        - RECRUITING: Currently recruiting participants
        - ACTIVE_NOT_RECRUITING: Active but not recruiting
        - COMPLETED: Study completed
        - ENROLLING_BY_INVITATION: Enrolling by invitation only
        - NOT_YET_RECRUITING: Not yet recruiting
        - SUSPENDED: Study suspended
        - TERMINATED: Study terminated
        - WITHDRAWN: Study withdrawn
        - AVAILABLE: Available
        - NO_LONGER_AVAILABLE: No longer available
        - TEMPORARILY_NOT_AVAILABLE: Temporarily not available
        - APPROVED_FOR_MARKETING: Approved for marketing
        - WITHHELD: Withheld
        - UNKNOWN: Unknown status

    StudyType:
        - INTERVENTIONAL: Interventional studies
        - OBSERVATIONAL: Observational studies
        - EXPANDED_ACCESS: Expanded access studies

    PrimaryPurpose:
        - TREATMENT: Treatment
        - PREVENTION: Prevention
        - DIAGNOSTIC: Diagnostic
        - ECT: Educational/Counseling/Training
        - SUPPORTIVE_CARE: Supportive Care
        - SCREENING: Screening
        - HEALTH_SERVICES_RESEARCH: Health Services Research

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

query.description:
Query to search for visual content in the document. If you know the specific
figure/table/formula you are looking for, you can specify it here (e.g. "find me
Figure 3" or "extract the table on page 10"). You can also request based on content
(e.g. "find me all volcano plots of gene X" or "I need the formula for the growth rate").
You can even include explicit instructions for the LLM agent to follow (if helpful, not
necessarily required). The more specific and clear your query is here, the higher the
chance of success.
query.title: Query

text_name.description: Name of a text chunk (e.g., 'smith2023example pages 1-5').
text_name.title: Text Name

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

artifact_type.description:
Artifact type to create. Must be one of: table,
code_block, blockquote, image.
artifact_type.title: Artifact Type

description.description:
Description of what you want in the artifact. Be specific
about what information should be included, how it should be organized,
and what columns/sections/content you want. This guides the summary LLM.
For image type, describe the visual you want generated in detail.
description.title: Description

info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation
history thus far, only the question and each text. Note that it only sees text, no images or other
media from the contents (though tables and formulae may be parseable in some cases).

Think of this tool as an efficient way to deeply scan all retrieved documents for evidence. It
is complementary to the `read_text` tool, which can be used to directly inspect a subset of the
retrieved documents.

A valuable time to invoke this tool is after another tool finds potentially relevant documents.
Feel free to invoke this tool in parallel with other tools, but do not call this tool in parallel with itself.
Only invoke this tool when the document count is above zero, or this tool will be useless.

If you call this tool 2+ times and repeatedly get 'No relevant evidence found',
consider whether the answer might be in visual content (figures/tables) rather than text,
and use appropriate tools if available to access that content.

Once you receive evidence from this tool:

1. Read Carefully: Don't skim. The evidence may contain multiple similar terms
   or values—make sure you identify the RIGHT one.

2. For Comparative Questions: If the question asks "which X has greatest Y",
   check that the evidence includes information about ALL relevant X options, not
   just one or two. If you only see partial information, gather more evidence.

3. Check for Noise: Verify that numbers or terms aren't just metadata
   (page numbers, reference IDs, dates). Look for the value in meaningful
   scientific context.

4. Context Matters: A term appearing 71 times doesn't mean it's always the answer.
   Verify which occurrence actually answers the question asked.

If the evidence doesn't clearly answer the question, gather more evidence before
concluding. Don't guess based on partial information.

question.description: Specific question to gather evidence for.
question.title: Question

text_name_focus_list.description:
if there are known text names that are relevant to the question,
you can specify them here. This will ensure that the tool will look at these text names
first, and then look at the rest of the evidence. If left as `None`, an embedding
search will be performed on underlying content to find most relevant texts.
text_name_focus_list.title: Text Name Focus List

info.name: update_plan
info.description:
Update the plan for a specific or new objective using a JSON string to create or
replace the existing objective.

The updated_json should be a JSON string representing a single plan objective object.

You may use this tool to update an objective, create a new one, or change
strategy if the current plan is not working. Only change strategy significantly
as a last resort, after trying very hard to make the current plan work.

Only mark an objective as completed if you are absolutely sure that it has been fully
met. If it is only partially met, you may add additional objectives to the plan for
what is missing.

plan_objective_id.description: The id of the objective to update.
plan_objective_id.title: Plan Objective Id

updated_plan_objective_json.description:
A JSON string representing the updated objective.
It should be a dictionary with the with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id matching plan_objective_id, if not found, a new objective is created.
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
updated_plan_objective_json.title: Updated Plan Objective Json

info.name: patent_search
info.description:
Search for patents to increase the patent count.

Repeat previous calls with the same query to continue a search.
Only repeat a maximum of three times.
This tool can be called concurrently.
This tool introduces novel patents, so invoke it when just beginning
or when unsatisfied with the current evidence.

query.description:
A search query for patents (using Google Patents). Never include temporal
filters here (e.g. specific years or dates); instead use the `after` and `before`
arguments. Never include author filters here; instead use the `inventor` argument.
Supports the following syntax, but they can be brittle and are not preferred; try
simple queries where possible:
- Boolean operators: AND (default), OR, and - (NOT)
- Exact phrases: "quoted text"
- Proximity: NEAR/x, ADJ/x (ordered), WITH (20 words), SAME (200 words)
- Field search: TI=(title), AB=(abstract), CL=(claims)
- CPC codes: cpc:A01B or CPC=B60R22/low (includes children)
- Wildcards: ? (0-1 char), * (0+ chars), # (exactly 1 char)
- Chemistry: exact molecule names, SSS=molecule (substructure),
  ~molecule (similar), SMILES strings, SMARTS=pattern, InChI keys,
  CL=~molecule (chemistry in claims)
query.title: Query

after.description:
Minimum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20150101' for patents after Jan 1, 2015.
after.title: After

before.description:
Maximum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20200101' for patents before Jan 1, 2020.
before.title: Before

date_type.description:
Type of date that after and before refer to. Must be either 'publication'
or 'filing'. Only necessary to set if after and/or before are set.
date_type.title: Date Type

inventor.description: Filter by inventor name(s). Comma-separated for multiple.
inventor.title: Inventor

Search for disease-target associations from OpenTargets database.

info.name: answer
info.description:
Submit your final answer to the user. You MUST call this tool on your final answer.
If you mark all objectives as completed but have not yet called this tool, then
the answer will not be submitted. Note that this tool should only be called once, as it
immediately terminates the run and submits the answer.

Write an answer based on the evidence from gather_evidence results in message history.
If the context provides insufficient information, provide a partial answer and explain
why it is partial (e.g. the question is currently an open question in the field,
you were unable to obtain certain papers, etc.).

For each part of your answer, indicate which sources most support it via citation IDs at
the end of sentences, like (pqac-0000ABCD).
You are only allowed to cite available context IDs, indicated in previous messages by "Context IDs that may be cited:".
## Valid citation examples, only use comma/space delimited parentheticals:

- (pqac-0000ABCD, pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000IJKL)

## Invalid citation examples:

- (pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD;pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD-pqac-0000EFGH)
- pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH
- Example's work pqac-0000ABCD
- (pages pqac-0000ABCD)
- ![description](pqac-0000ABCD)
- ()

Do not concatenate citation ids, just use them as-is.

When writing your answer, embed artifacts if relevant artifacts have been previously
created by the `create_artifact` tool. To embed an artifact, simply include this in your
answer, on its own line and without any additional formatting (i.e. no backticks, code fences,
quotes, additional tags, etc.).
Always provide at least some introductory sentence or paragraph before referring to an artifact,
so that the artifact is properly contextualized.
Here is an example reference to an artifact with ID "artifact-XY":
<artifact id="artifact-XY"/>

Valid artifact IDs are indicated in previous messages by 'Artifact IDs that may be injected into the answer:'.


Double-check your answer:

1. Evidence Match: Re-read the specific evidence snippets you're citing. Does your
   answer actually match what they say? Don't rely on memory from 20+ messages ago.

2. For Comparative Questions ("which X has greatest/maximum/highest Y"):
   - Did you examine ALL options mentioned in the evidence?
   - Did you explicitly compare their values?
   - Example: If evidence mentions "Pancreatic: 0.92, Liver: 0.85, Lung: 0.78",
     verify you compared all three, not just two.

3. For Specific Value Questions ("How many", "What is the", specific terms):
   - Does the exact value you're stating appear in the evidence?
   - Are you extracting from the right context (not noise like page numbers)?

4. Sanity Check: Read your answer. Does it directly address what was asked?

Don't use Markdown image syntax like ![...](...) to reference media in your answer,
because media get automatically linked by the system based on your answer's citations.

Write in the style of a scientific article, with concise sentences and
coherent paragraphs. This answer will be used directly,
so do not add any extraneous information.

answer.description: valid answer, cited with citation IDs.
answer.title: Answer

messages.content:
Use the tools to answer the question: What do recent (2023-2026) reviews, perspectives and roadmap papers identify as the OPEN PROBLEMS and FUTURE DIRECTIONS for self-driving laboratories, specifically in materials chemistry and electrochemistry? Give DOIs. I want the concrete, named challenges rather than generalities: orchestration/interoperability standards (SiLA2, LabOP, AnIML, Bluesky, Chemputer/chi), FAIR data and metadata capture, reproducibility and round-robin benchmarking between labs, the shortage of negative results, closing the loop with multiple ORTHOGONAL characterization modalities rather than a single scalar objective, multi-fidelity and multi-objective optimization, transfer/meta-learning across chemistries, human-in-the-loop and error recovery, and cost/accessibility. Abstract:
<jats:p>Scientific discovery is fundamentally a problem-solving process involving distributed intelligence. Human intuition, computational reasoning, and experimental execution are distributed across people, instruments, and software systems, limiting the speed and scale of discovery. Although automation, high-throughput experimentation, foundation models, and cloud infrastructure have accelerated individual stages of the scientific workflow, they have not unified the discovery process. We hypothesize that the next generation of laboratories will be agentic: environments in which scientists, AI systems, and robotic platforms operate as collaborative discovery partners, with humans contributing the parts of discovery that remain hardest to make explicit: asking the right questions and holding provisional mechanistic models of how a system works. The key missing layer is an agentic harnessing layer that continuously integrates hypothesis, literature-derived evidence, experimental data, uncertainty, and experimental state into a shared “laboratory world model”—a dynamic representation of the scientific system and its evolving context. By maintaining and updating this lab world model, the agentic harnessing layer enables coordinated decision-making, adaptive planning, and increasingly autonomous scientific workflows across humans and machines. A central challenge is that much of the scientific research process remains inaccessible to machines, including tacit knowledge, human observations, adaptive decision-making, and evolving experimental context. Advances in multimodal AI and immersive interfaces may help bridge this gap, allowing humans, agents, and robotic systems to collaborate seamlessly in scientific discovery rather than simply automating isolated tasks. Agentic laboratories could provide a new architecture for science, integrating human, artificial, and physical intelligence into a unified discovery system.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>In iterative optimization, actions are adjusted based on what we see—such as dosing until dissolution or stirring until mixing is complete. Self-driving laboratories (SDLs) offer an opportunity to guide experimental adjustments based on such visual feedback in an autonomous, iterative way. However, current SDLs do not monitor these visual cues. HeinSight 4.0 fills this gap by integrating computer vision into SDLs to enable real-time experimental adjustments based on visual feedback. The computer vision detects equipment (e.g., reactor, vial), classifies chemical phases (solid, liquid, air), and analyzes image features such as turbidity and color. HeinSight 4.0 tracks these physical characteristics frame by frame and interprets physical states (e.g., dissolution, separation). This data feeds into a rule-based system that integrates with the SDL to make real-time experimental adjustments. We demonstrate HeinSight 4.0 adaptability across two pharmaceutical case studies: purification (solubility screening) and drug formulation (melt spray congeal). We also developed a hardware-agnostic architecture and deployed it across two institutions with distinct robotic systems. The open-source HeinSight 4.0 enables SDLs to see, think, and act in real time.</jats:p>

                  <jats:p>Polymeric materials underpin modern technologies spanning energy storage, microelectronics, healthcare and sustainable manufacturing. Yet their rational design remains exceptionally challenging because material performance emerges from complex interactions among molecular composition, chain architecture, processing history and hierarchical structural evolution across multiple length and time scales. Consequently, polymer research has long relied on labor-intensive experimentation and fragmented modeling approaches, limiting both mechanistic understanding and innovation efficiency. Recent advances in data infrastructure, machine learning, large artificial intelligence (AI) models and laboratory automation are beginning to reshape this landscape. Rather than functioning as isolated tools, polymer databases, predictive models, AI agents and automated laboratories are increasingly converging into interconnected discovery ecosystems. As a result, the central challenge is shifting from improving predictive accuracy alone to enabling reliable decision-making, adaptive learning and seamless integration across computation, experimentation and scientific reasoning. We argue that polymer science is entering an era of autonomous discovery, in which data, simulation, reasoning and experimentation operate within self-improving feedback loops that continuously generate hypotheses, design materials, execute experiments and refine predictive models. By unifying molecular design, process optimization, experimental validation and industrial translation, such autonomous ecosystems establish a more predictive, reproducible and scalable paradigm for polymer innovation, fundamentally transforming how polymer research is conducted.</jats:p>

Halide perovskites (HPs) are emerging as key materials in the fight against global warming with well recognized applications, such as photovoltaics, and emergent opportunities, such as photocatalysis for methane removal and environmental remediation. These current and emergent applications are enabled by a unique combination of high absorption coefficients, tunable band gaps, and long carrier diffusion lengths, making them highly efficient for solar energy conversion. To address the challenge of discovery and optimization of HPs in huge chemical and compositional spaces of possible candidates, this perspective discusses a comprehensive strategy for screening HPs through automated high-throughput and combinatorial synthesis techniques. A critical aspect of this approach is closing the characterization loop, where machine learning (ML) and human collaboration play pivotal roles. By leveraging human creativity and domain knowledge for hypothesis generation and employing ML to test and refine these hypotheses efficiently, we aim to accelerate the discovery and optimization of HPs under specific environmental conditions. This synergy enables rapid identification of the most promising materials, advancing from fundamental discovery to scalable manufacturability. Our ultimate goal of this work is to transition from laboratory-scale innovations to real-world applications, ensuring that HPs can be deployed effectively in technologies that mitigate global warming, such as in solar energy harvesting and methane removal systems.

<jats:p>The production of green hydrogen through water splitting requires highly efficient electrocatalysts, but the current trial-and-error-based synthesis or discovery is time-consuming, costly and resource-intensive. Machine learning (ML) provides a powerful, data-driven alternative that can model complex structure-activity relationships across large chemical spaces at orders-of-magnitude speed. This review systematically overviews the life cycle of the electrocatalyst research and development application of ML. First, the thermodynamic and kinetic principles of the hydrogen and oxygen evolution reactions are summarised, along with some well-adopted and accepted activity descriptors. Then we explore data sources, featurization approaches, and algorithms, and discuss the model space, from a simple interpretable model to a graph neural network to a generative model, in the context of the ML toolkit. Strategic applications are discussed for high-throughput virtual screening of alloys and single-atom catalysts, as well as multifunctional activity prediction for overall water splitting, and stability optimisation under operating conditions. The topic of emerging frontiers is highlighted, including high-entropy alloys, amorphous materials, and linking atomic-scale understanding to device-level performance through integration with density functional theory. Finally, the problems of data scarcity, model interpretability and the discrepancy between computational predictions and industrial implementation are discussed, along with future directions for closed-loop discovery and self-driving laboratories. Incorporating ML into electrocatalyst design and combining it with autonomous experimentation will revolutionise this process, from simulation to energy solution, dramatically speeding it up.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>The solid-state electrolytes (SSE) are gaining tremendous attention in designing rechargeable batteries with remarkable energy density and safety features for next-generation energy storage device applications. The rational design of SSE with promising ionic conductivity, higher electrochemical stability windows, and stable electrode-electrolyte interfaces remain a formidable challenge, traditionally hindered by trial-and-error experimentation and computationally expensive theoretical simulations. Here, we systematically review the recent breakthroughs in the artificial intelligence (AI)-driven design of SSE, spanning electrochemical stability and ionic conductivity domains, with a particular focus on how machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) are fundamentally transforming the discovery and optimization landscape. We critically discuss the synergy between first-principles density functional theory (DFT), molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, and advanced AI algorithms including supervised and unsupervised learning (SL, UL), graph neural networks (GNNs), and Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials (MLIP) that collectively enable accurate prediction of ionic conductivity, elucidation of ion transport mechanisms, and high-throughput screening (HTS) of vast chemical spaces. Emphasis is placed on descriptor engineering that bridges atomic-level structural features (e.g., lattice parameters, activation energies, defect chemistry) with macroscopic electrochemical performance, as well as the emerging paradigm of closed-loop, self-driving laboratories for autonomous materials discovery. Furthermore, AI-guided strategies have demonstrated remarkable interfacial ionic transport mechanism. Despite these transformative advances, persistent challenges including data scarcity, limited descriptor transferability, discrepancies between theoretical predictions and experimental realization, remain significant challenges. Looking forward, the convergence of AI with high-throughput experimentation and multiscale modeling promises to redefine SSE discovery, accelerating the deployment of high-performance all solid-state batteries (ASSBs) for sustainable energy storage.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Self-driving laboratories (SDLs) promise an accelerated application of the scientific method. Through the automation of experimental workflows, along with autonomous experimental planning, SDLs hold the potential to greatly accelerate research in chemistry and materials discovery. This review provides an in-depth analysis of the state-of-the-art in SDL technology, its applications across various scientific disciplines, and the potential implications for research and industry. Abstract:
<jats:p>Discovering new high-performance materials and alloys is often likened to finding a needle in a haystack because the design space of chemical compositions and processing conditions is astronomically large, and the discovery process is laborious and prohibitively costly. This perspective articulates a research agenda for autonomous materials and metallurgy discovery platforms that combine closed-loop machine learning with robotic experimentation and traditional materials engineering precepts to formulate, process, and test candidate materials with reduced human intervention, and to iterate recursively for stepwise optimization. It explores how sequential learning methods, generative modeling, and hybrid model-based strategies can analyze multimodal experimental data and propose new compositions and processing schedules for subsequent experiments. This approach has the potential to considerably accelerate the pace of discoveries, from decades to mere weeks. Representation learning for material formulations, the injection of domain knowledge into decision-making, and the mechatronic design of robotics that can safely execute harsh processing are all explored as essential components in closing the autonomous loop. Surveyed exemplars show order-of-magnitude improvements in experimental throughput and discovery efficiency. Furthermore, the paper proposes a multidimensional framework for classifying and evaluating the autonomy, complexity, and integration levels of self-driving laboratories, intended to give researchers and practitioners a structured approach to benchmarking future developments in the field. The perspective concludes with an analysis of data infrastructure, simulation coupling, robustness, and human-machine collaboration, distilled into a structured research agenda whose pursuit would broaden adoption across energy, aerospace, and other sectors.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The chemical and biochemical sciences are undergoing a profound digital transformation that is giving rise to the emerging paradigm of the digital analytical sciences, driven by an increasing need for research data digitalization, structuring, and standardization. This Trends article provides a bird’s-eye view of how FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) data ecosystems are evolving from administrative guidelines into a critical enabler of modern analytical discovery. Because major advances in artificial intelligence (AI) depend fundamentally on structured and openly accessible scientific data, we discuss how the analytical sciences are now laying the corresponding infrastructural foundations needed to support the next generation of data-driven research. However, in domains such as biophotonics and advanced spectroscopy, large, comprehensively annotated experimental datasets remain limited, and algorithmic advances alone cannot fully compensate for data scarcity or poor standardization. To address this challenge, we examine the rapidly emerging field of physics-informed deep learning, in which physical laws and domain knowledge are incorporated directly into AI pipelines. By leveraging quantum-chemical simulations and transfer-matrix optics to generate synthetic pretraining data, these hybrid approaches can improve the robustness and generalizability of predictive models trained on limited experimental datasets. Finally, we discuss the emerging role of scientific representation learning and argue that realizing the full potential of AI in chemistry will require continued advances in hybrid algorithms alongside a sustained commitment to FAIR data governance and open scientific data infrastructures.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>Large language model (LLM)-based agents can increasingly support and empower human scientists in their work by reading literature, generating hypotheses, designing experiments, analyzing data, interpreting results, and drafting manuscripts. In parallel, robotics and programmable, cloud-connected laboratories have the potential to transform wet-lab operations into software-addressable infrastructure. Yet biological experiments face a persistent reality gap in which silent failures, temporal drift, contamination, sample mix-ups, and ambiguous protocol intent can invalidate an otherwise sound experimental plan. Closing this gap is essential for bringing the speed of modern computational discovery to experimental biology and requires audit-grade execution and verification. Here, we distinguish scripted automation from flexible, AI-enabled autonomy and outline a staged roadmap toward human-led and trustworthy “self-driving” labs for biology. We define laboratory autonomy in the context of a human-led scientific endeavor as a bounded control loop in which scientists set goals and constraints, agents help plan and coordinate experiments, instruments execute experiments and report machine-checkable evidence, and humans verify and interpret results and govern high-consequence decisions. We discuss where such systems are most appropriate and relevant today and where caution or deferral is needed. We map key lab-side potential failure modes and argue for verifiability-first autonomy. If developed responsibly, such systems could enable scientists to more efficiently decipher combinatorially large perturbation, design, and optimization spaces that are currently impractical to test experimentally, while empowering, rather than replacing, human creativity and judgment in experimental biological discovery.</jats:p>

Abstract:
In this work, we highlight the need for dynamic workflow managers in self‐driving laboratories (SDLs) and optimizers for Materials Acceleration Platforms (MAPs). While MAPs leverage artificial intelligence (AI) and automation to accelerate materials discovery, static workflow managers limit scalability, and flexibility. We demonstrate the benefits of modular, adaptable orchestrators by integrating PerQueue, a dynamic workflow manager, into a color‐mixing robot, streamlining task coordination and AI‐driven optimization. Additionally, we assess various MAP‐relevant methodologies based on their maturity and readiness for integration. This assessment underlines the importance of flexible workflow managers in advancing SDLs and optimizers, paving the way for more effective future MAP implementations. Achieving seamless integration requires addressing challenges like ensuring data provenance, adhering to findable, accessible, interoperable, reusable principles, and adapting workflows to changing experimental conditions—key elements for the successful deployment of MAPs.

The development of automated high-throughput experimental platforms has enabled fast sampling of high-dimensional decision spaces. To reach target properties efficiently, these platforms are increasingly paired with intelligent experimental design. However, current optimizers show limitations in maintaining sufficient exploration/exploitation balance for problems dealing with multiple conflicting objectives and complex constraints. Here, we devised an Evolution-Guided Bayesian Optimization (EGBO) algorithm that integrates selection pressure in parallel with a q-Noisy Expected Hypervolume Improvement (qNEHVI) optimizer; this not only solves for the Pareto Front (PF) efficiently but also achieves better coverage of the PF while limiting sampling in the infeasible space. The algorithm was developed together with a custom self-driving lab for seed-mediated silver nanoparticle synthesis, targeting 3 objectives (1) optical properties, (2) fast reaction, and (3) minimal seed usage alongside complex constraints. We demonstrated that, with appropriate constraint handling, EGBO performance improves upon state-of-the-art qNEHVI. Furthermore, across various synthetic multi-objective problems, EGBO showed significative hypervolume improvement, revealing the synergy between selection pressure and the qNEHVI optimizer. We also demonstrated EGBO’s good coverage of the PF as well as comparatively better ability to propose feasible solutions. We thus propose EGBO as a general framework for efficiently solving constrained multi-objective problems in high-throughput experimentation platforms.

Experience-driven optimization has been pivotal in advancing organic photovoltaics, where chemically intuitive and stepwise tuning of processing parameters can yield high-performance organic solar cells (OSCs). However, systematically locating optimal regions under high-dimensional, strongly coupled, and multi-objective constraints remains challenging across diverse scenarios. Here, we introduce a closed-loop workflow base on multi-objective Bayesian optimization for efficient process optimization of OSCs. Applied to a quaternary system comprising the widely used polymer donors PM6 and D18 and the non-fullerene acceptors BTP-eC9 and L8BO, the workflow navigates an eight-dimensional space jointly defined by composition and fabrication variables, encompassing 2.2 × 10 14 possible combinations. Within five active-learning cycles, the search rapidly converges to a high-performance region, achieving a power conversion efficiency exceeding 20% while drastically reducing the time and effort compared to conventional trial-and-error approaches. The generalizability of the workflow is further demonstrated across different material systems and fabrication methods, consistently guiding the optimization toward high-performance regions in only a few iterations. This work establishes a generalizable, efficient, and scalable closed-loop framework for the rapid identification of optimal process windows in high-dimensional, multi-objective systems for organic photovoltaics and beyond.

The excerpt identifies open problems that bear directly on materials-chemistry self-driving laboratories, although it does not discuss every named standard or method individually. Interoperability and orchestration require machine-readable, sufficiently explicit procedures that retain platform identity, instrument configuration, calibration state, software versions, deviations, and raw analytical evidence; abstraction that is too general can create reproducibility debt. FAIR data challenges include incomplete metadata about preparation, environment, instrument state, unsuccessful procedures, and manual interventions, making it difficult to distinguish chemistry from instrumentation or procedural drift. Benchmarking and round-robin validation remain difficult because simulations cannot reproduce all laboratory failures; planners need prospective tests involving noise, constraints, missing measurements, failed runs, and distributional change. The article emphasizes that data volume is insufficient and that negative or failed experiments must be interpretable. More broadly, biological and complex materials systems create delayed outcomes, variability, and incomplete representations, complicating multimodal closed-loop control. Optimization must accommodate mixed variables, discontinuities, changing objectives, constraints, cost, and multiobjective trade-offs rather than assume interchangeable queries. Transfer across chemistries is limited: optimizers require context-specific qualification and requalification. Human oversight, safe recovery, escalation, provenance, and challenge rights remain essential. Finally, distributed access raises coordination, cybersecurity, fidelity, scheduling, maintenance, and equity issues, while evaluation must include resource use and downstream scientific or pharmaceutical impact, not merely speed.

The excerpt identifies several open problems for materials-chemistry self-driving laboratories. Data infrastructure is a central challenge: autonomous-lab data are often stored in bespoke, siloed formats, so the field needs agreed schemas and ontologies aligned with FAIR principles to enable cross-lab data fusion and reusable models. Physical experiments remain costly and slow, motivating tightly coupled multi-fidelity simulations and digital twins, with AI deciding whether to run inexpensive virtual or definitive physical experiments. Generalisation across chemistries is limited by platform specialisation, re-tooling expense, and the cold-start problem; transfer learning and foundation models are proposed solutions, subject to data-poisoning risks. Reliable unattended operation requires real-time detection of experimental errors, sensor drift, and mechanical failures, plus self-calibration and fail-safe recovery. Safety guardrails and mandatory human review are also needed. Finally, current systems largely optimise known parameters; open-ended discovery requires curiosity-driven objectives, generative models, and uncertainty-aware active learning. The excerpt stresses that human scientists should remain collaborators, with explainable AI supporting hypothesis formation and scientific understanding. The excerpt frames the major open problems for self-driving laboratories as socio-technical and evidentiary, rather than merely engineering limitations. Reliable acceleration depends on valid measurements, robust experiment planning and execution, explicit uncertainty handling, complete provenance, reproducible protocols, and effective human escalation. Closed-loop systems can instead amplify biased data, proxy objectives, analytical drift, brittle abstractions, and overconfident models. For distributed or remotely accessible laboratories, cross-platform transfer, provenance completeness, security, and protocol-equivalence testing are highlighted; platform heterogeneity may undermine reproducibility. Abstract:
<jats:p>Low-cost self-driving labs (SDLs) offer faster prototyping, low-risk hands-on experience, and a test bed for sophisticated experimental planning software which helps us develop state-of-the-art SDLs.</jats:p>

Relevant Snippet:
This review proposes the concept of a “frugal twin,” similar to a digital twin, but for physical experiments. Frugal twins range from simple toy examples to low-cost surrogates of high-cost research systems. For example, a color-mixing self-driving laboratory (SDL) can serve as a low-cost version of a costly multi-step chemical discovery SDL. Frugal twins already provide hands-on experience for SDLs with low costs and low risks. They can also offer as test beds for software prototyping (e.g., optimization, data infrastructure), and a low barrier to entry for democratizing SDLs. However, there is room for improvement. The true value of frugal twins can be realized in three core areas. Firstly, hardware and software modularity; secondly, purpose-built design (human-inspired vs. hardware-centric vs. human-in-the-loop); and thirdly state-of-the-art (SOTA) software (e.g., multi-fidelity optimization). We also describe the ethical benefits and risks that come with the democratization of science through frugal twins. For future work, we suggest ideas for new frugal twins, SDL educational course outcomes, and a classification scheme for autonomy levels.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Next-generation autonomous laboratories that combine machine learning, robotic synthesis, and in situ characterization is rapidly emerging as one of the key directions in modern materials science. By integrating active and deep learning algorithms with multi-level datasets ranging from quantum mechanical simulations to high-throughput flow-based experiments, these platforms establish closed-loop frameworks that guide complex nanofabrication processes in real time. Such AI-driven systems lower material and energy consumption, enable the precise design of nanostructures with tailored optical, electronic, and mechanical properties, and create research opportunities that were previously difficult to realize. This review provides a comprehensive overview of self-driving laboratories (SDLs), including their architectures, algorithmic strategies, and practical demonstrations such as the optimization of perovskite nanostructures, the development of nanoparticles for targeted drug delivery, and the synthesis of quantum dots with controlled emission. It also discusses existing methodological limitations, the need for standardized data practices, and challenges related to the integration of in situ techniques, while highlighting the prospects for creating fully digital pipelines for material production, as evidenced by recent autonomous laboratory demonstrations that progressed from initial hypotheses to functional prototypes within remarkably short timeframes.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>The discovery of next-generation battery electrolytes increasingly involves complex, multicomponent formulations that demand high-throughput, systematic exploration. We present the Bayesian Robotic Investigator of Novel Electrolytes (BRINE), a cost-effective, self-driving laboratory (SDL) that autonomously prepares and tests mixed electrolyte solutions. BRINE combines an open-source liquid-handling robot with a potentiostat and custom-made electrodes to mix reagents and perform electrochemical measurements without human intervention. A Bayesian optimization routine navigates multidimensional composition spaces, allowing the platform to rapidly identify promising formulations. As a proof of concept, BRINE mapped ionic conductivity in two aqueous electrolyte spaces (i) aqueous mixtures of NaCl, KCl, MgCl2, and CaCl2, and (ii) battery-oriented mixtures containing ZnCl2, KCl, NH4Cl, NaCl, and EMIMCl, testing ~230 unique compositions in under 18 hours and finding conductivities up to 32.13 S/m. These results demonstrate how closed-loop autonomous experimentation and optimization accelerate the identification of electrolytes with the highest conductivity across a large multicomponent composition space, while minimizing experimental variability. This work lays the foundation for broader electrochemical studies using the BRINE platform.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>Chemical-enhanced oil recovery (EOR) is a field of study that can gain significantly from artificial intelligence (AI), addressing uncertainties such as mobility control, interfacial tension reduction, wettability alteration, and emulsifications. The primary objective of this paper is to introduce an integrated framework for AI and chemical EOR for energy harvest operations. Central emphasis is placed on the energy transition, with the aim of expediting the development of cleaner energy harvesting systems and attaining the goal of net-zero emission. To do so, we present how the energy transition is changing the manufacturing of the chemicals for EOR application. For this, the uncertainty associated with materials' design and critical role of the simulators for transferring the laboratory experiences into full-field implementations is discussed. The concept of digitalization and its impact on energy companies are highlighted. The role of digital twin in simulators integration is discussed, emphasizing how increased data access can help design more tolerant chemicals for harsh reservoir environments using real-time data. Also, we discuss how the chemical suppliers, research institutes, startups, and field operators can benefit from self-leaning and robotic laboratories for chemicals manufacturing. Moreover, this paper explores how including AI perspectives can improve our understanding of developing chemical formulations by blending hybrid capabilities. This approach contributes to making energy production more sustainable and aligning with the goal of zero emissions. A workflow is presented to demonstrate how the integration of AI and chemical EOR can be used for both hydrocarbon production and other energy transition operations, such as carbon capture, utilization and storage, hydrogen storage, and geothermal reservoirs. The outcome of this paper stands as a pioneering effort that uniquely addresses these challenges for both academia and the industry and can open many additional doors and identify topics requiring further investigations.

                  <jats:p>This study explores how artificial intelligence (AI) is being used to support more sustainable production systems in chemical engineering. It combines bibliometric analysis with machine learning techniques to examine how research in this area has developed and where it is heading. Bibliometric analysis is used to map the global research landscape of AI-related sustainability studies, revealing key research themes, collaboration networks, and leading countries and institutions. Visual analyses generated using VOSviewer demonstrate the prominent role of AI-based analytical methods in chemical engineering applications such as industrial process optimization, environmental monitoring, and resource-efficient production. Alongside this, the study presents a targeted review of 113 peer-reviewed publications from a chemical engineering perspective, focusing on major application areas including sustainable manufacturing, wastewater treatment and membrane technologies, renewable energy systems, energy storage optimization, and sustainable supply chain management. Machine learning methods are also used to analyze changes over time and to provide an indication of future research directions. Overall, the findings show that AI is playing an increasingly important role in improving efficiency, flexibility, and sustainability across different stages of production. This work offers a structured overview of current developments and highlights opportunities for future research and practical implementation in sustainable chemical engineering systems.</jats:p>

The excerpt identifies six defining characteristics of SDL 2.0: interoperability, collaboration, generalizability, orchestration, safety, and creativity. Interoperability requires shared metadata schemas, chemistry and materials ontologies, machine-readable vocabularies, version-controlled and provenance-tracked digital recipes, hardware-agnostic normalization, reference experiments, calibration materials, and protocols for exchanging tagged samples. These standards would enable distributed laboratories to share validated workflows, combine datasets, perform large-scale meta-analysis, and train more generalizable models. Collaboration should emphasize user-friendly interfaces, natural-language or drag-and-drop workflow design, explainable and uncertainty-aware AI, graduated autonomy, human checkpoints, and the ability to modify rewards, add hypotheses, or halt unsafe experiments. Orchestration is framed through intelligent scheduling that reduces bottlenecks and resource conflicts; safety through proactive protocols and expert review; creativity through testing novel hypotheses; and generalizability through shared, cross-laboratory data and models. Major access problems include the computational expense of generative models and the concentration of advanced tools in well-funded institutions, motivating lightweight or cloud alternatives and open, interoperable platforms. This excerpt does not specifically discuss negative-result reporting or round-robin benchmarking, although it does call for reference experiments and calibration materials to benchmark reproducibility.

{"artifact_type": "table", "description": "Create a comprehensive summary table of the 9 open problems/challenges for self-driving laboratories in materials chemistry and electrochemistry. For each challenge, include:
1. Challenge name (exactly as listed by the user)
2. Status as of 2026 (all are UNSOLVED but have varying degrees of partial progress)
3. Key issues identified in the literature
4. Key references with DOIs

The 9 challenges are:
1. Orchestration/interoperability standards (SiLA2, LabOP, AnIML, Bluesky, Chemputer/chi) - UNSOLVED. No universally adopted standard; SiLA2 and OPC UA gaining traction but instrument manufacturers lack APIs; materials ontologies immature (Tom et al. 10.1021/acs.chemrev.4c00055; Lee et al. 10.1039/d5mh01984b; Steensen et al. 10.1002/aidi.202500067)
2. FAIR data and metadata capture - UNSOLVED. Data fragmented across bespoke formats; Matryoshka files and SEARS proposed but not community-wide; incomplete metadata on preparation, environment, instrument state (Gauthier et al. 10.1039/d5dd00297d; Tali et al. 10.1039/d5dd00175g; Hao et al. 10.51847/i178allztd)
3. Reproducibility and round-robin benchmarking - UNSOLVED. No formal inter-lab round-robin protocols; LLM nondeterminism threatens reproducibility; prospective challenge sets and independent replication called for but not established (Hao et al. 10.51847/i178allztd; Silva et al. 10.2172/3377973; Mallia & Caputo 10.69709/caic.2026.133382)
4. Shortage of negative results - UNSOLVED. Chemical databases emphasize successes; failed experiments not routinely captured or published; essential for model training and avoiding bias (Gauthier et al. 10.1039/d5dd00297d; Hao et al. 10.51847/i178allztd)
5. Closing the loop with multiple orthogonal characterization modalities - UNSOLVED. Most SDLs optimize a single scalar; integrating XRD, spectroscopy, microscopy, electrochemistry requires data fusion, uncertainty calibration, and decision models; missing/incomplete data across modalities (Wakabayashi & Otsuka 10.48550/arxiv.2608.26016; Foadian et al. 10.1021/acsmaterialsau.4c00096; Müller et al. 10.48550/arxiv.2609.04564)
6. Multi-fidelity and multi-objective optimization - UNSOLVED. Low-fidelity measurements may be weakly correlated or biased; Pareto-front acquisition is complex; scalarization compresses trade-offs; cost-aware acquisition functions needed (Wakabayashi & Otsuka 10.48550/arxiv.2608.26016; Hippalgaonkar et al. 10.21203/rs.3.rs-3578558/v1)
7. Transfer/meta-learning across chemistries - UNSOLVED. Negative transfer risk when source/target systems differ; experimental drift, batch effects, instrument differences; warm starts require compatible inputs/objectives; few systematic demonstrations (Wakabayashi & Otsuka 10.48550/arxiv.2608.26016; Mallia & Caputo 10.69709/caic.2026.133382; Bennett et al. 10.1038/s41467-026-74425-x)
8. Human-in-the-loop and error recovery - UNSOLVED. Silent failures, sensor drift, reagent degradation; no standardized escalation or recovery protocols; human oversight needed for goals, constraints, safety; LLM agents can hallucinate or make unsafe proposals (Cheng et al. 10.20944/preprints202608.0273.v1; Hao et al. 10.51847/i178allztd; Lee et al. 10.1039/d5mh01984b)
9. Cost/accessibility - UNSOLVED. Multi-million dollar/euro investments concentrated in elite institutions; frugal twins from ~$100-$30,000 proposed but limited capability; cloud labs help but have infrastructure costs; global equity gap (Lo et al. 10.1039/d3dd00223c; Mallia & Caputo 10.69709/caic.2026.133382; Jiang et al. 10.4208/cicc.2025.90.03)"}

messages.content:
### Artifact (ID artifact-00)

| Challenge | Status as of 2026 | Concrete unresolved issues identified in the literature | Key references and DOIs |
|---|---|---|---|
| Orchestration/interoperability standards (SiLA2, LabOP, AnIML, Bluesky, Chemputer/chi) | **UNSOLVED — partial, fragmented progress** | No universally adopted interface spans instruments, workflow descriptions, analytical formats, and orchestration layers. Vendor instruments often lack standardized APIs; static task graphs cannot reliably branch, resume, reallocate resources, or respond to drift; materials ontologies remain immature and weakly adopted. SiLA2/SiLA and OPC UA are promising device interfaces, AnIML addresses analytical data, LabOP and Chemputer/XDL represent procedures, and Bluesky provides acquisition orchestration—but the literature does **not** establish end-to-end interoperability among them or with `chi`. Syntactic portability also does not guarantee chemically equivalent execution across platforms. (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000014, pqac-00000033, pqac-00000037) | Tom et al., [10.1021/acs.chemrev.4c00055](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.chemrev.4c00055); Lee et al., [10.1039/d5mh01984b](https://doi.org/10.1039/d5mh01984b); Steensen et al., [10.1002/aidi.202500067](https://doi.org/10.1002/aidi.202500067); Jiang et al., [10.4208/cicc.2025.90.03](https://doi.org/10.4208/cicc.2025.90.03) |
| FAIR data and metadata capture | **UNSOLVED — working exemplars exist, not community-wide infrastructure** | Data remain fragmented across bespoke instrument files and laboratory schemas. A reusable record must bind raw traces to reagents and batch IDs, preparation history, environment, calibration and instrument state, software/model versions, preprocessing, branching decisions, manual interventions, failures, and uncertainty. Matryoshka files, semantic RDF/SHACL pipelines, SEARS, ontologies, and knowledge graphs demonstrate possible implementations, but ontology adoption and integration into live campaigns remain limited; some semantic conversion is still post hoc. (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000010, pqac-00000012, pqac-00000015) | Gauthier et al., [10.1039/d5dd00297d](https://doi.org/10.1039/d5dd00297d); Tali et al., [10.1039/d5dd00175g](https://doi.org/10.1039/d5dd00175g); Hao et al., [10.51847/i178allztd](https://doi.org/10.51847/i178allztd); Steensen et al., [10.1002/aidi.202500067](https://doi.org/10.1002/aidi.202500067) |
| Reproducibility and round-robin benchmarking between labs | **UNSOLVED — requirements proposed; accepted round-robin regime absent** | The field lacks standard multi-lab challenge sets and formal round-robin protocols that test the same recipes, samples, calibrants, and decision policies across heterogeneous platforms. Needed tests include prospective and independent replication, protocol-equivalence checks, orthogonal confirmation, long-duration campaigns, drift and missing-data stress tests, failed runs, distribution shifts, and comparisons with human-directed workflows. Agent/LLM nondeterminism adds a requirement to preserve prompts, plans, tool calls, approvals, environments, model/data versions, uncertainty, and recovery traces—not merely final outputs. (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000024, pqac-00000025, pqac-00000027, pqac-00000030) | Hao et al., [10.51847/i178allztd](https://doi.org/10.51847/i178allztd); Silva et al., [10.2172/3377973](https://doi.org/10.2172/3377973); Mallia and Caputo, [10.69709/caic.2026.133382](https://doi.org/10.69709/caic.2026.133382); Lee et al., [10.1039/d5mh01984b](https://doi.org/10.1039/d5mh01984b) |
| Shortage of negative results | **UNSOLVED — technically capturable, culturally and infrastructurally underreported** | Chemical datasets disproportionately retain successful outcomes, while failed synthesis, null measurements, infeasible regions, aborted runs, and troubleshooting decisions are omitted or collapsed into ambiguous zeros. This biases models and acquisition policies and prevents systems from distinguishing bad chemistry from analytical or robotic failure. Future records must preserve interpretable negative outcomes with raw evidence, failure taxonomy, provenance, and recovery actions. (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000004, pqac-00000006, pqac-00000012, pqac-00000015) | Gauthier et al., [10.1039/d5dd00297d](https://doi.org/10.1039/d5dd00297d); Hao et al., [10.51847/i178allztd](https://doi.org/10.51847/i178allztd) |
| Closing the loop with multiple ORTHOGONAL characterization modalities rather than a single scalar objective | **UNSOLVED — isolated multimodal demonstrations, no general fusion-and-decision framework** | XRD, spectroscopy, microscopy, electrochemistry, imaging, process logs, and device tests observe different material states and arrive with different noise, cost, delay, scale, and missingness. SDLs must link every derived objective to raw signals and quality controls, diagnose modality-specific failure, reconcile conflicting evidence, and choose whether the next action should optimize performance, reduce uncertainty, repeat a measurement, or invoke another modality. Reducing all evidence to one scalar can hide phase purity, degradation, mechanism, stability, or analytical failure. (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000018, pqac-00000040, pqac-00000041, pqac-00000042) | Wakabayashi and Otsuka, [10.48550/arXiv.2608.26016](https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2608.26016); Foadian et al., [10.1021/acsmaterialsau.4c00096](https://doi.org/10.1021/acsmaterialsau.4c00096); Müller et al., [10.48550/arXiv.2609.04564](https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2609.04564); Hao et al., [10.51847/i178allztd](https://doi.org/10.51847/i178allztd) |
| Multi-fidelity and multi-objective optimization | **UNSOLVED — algorithms exist, robust laboratory deployment remains problem-specific** | Multi-fidelity planners must learn source-specific bias and correlation and decide when a cheap simulation, proxy assay, or short electrochemical test is informative enough to defer an expensive synthesis, microscopy session, or long-duration cycling test. Weakly correlated fidelities can waste budget. Multi-objective campaigns must handle conflicting properties, feasibility and safety constraints, noisy outputs, asynchronous batches, replicates, and changing objectives. Scalarization can erase Pareto trade-offs; hypervolume methods become costly and sensitive to modeling assumptions. (pqac-00000018, pqac-00000020, pqac-00000021, pqac-00000022, pqac-00000046) | Wakabayashi and Otsuka, [10.48550/arXiv.2608.26016](https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2608.26016); Hippalgaonkar et al., [10.21203/rs.3.rs-3578558/v1](https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-3578558/v1); Lo et al., [10.1039/d3dd00223c](https://doi.org/10.1039/d3dd00223c) |
| Transfer/meta-learning across chemistries | **UNSOLVED — promising within related campaigns; cross-chemistry generalization unproven** | Warm starts require compatible descriptors, objectives, scales, constraints, and failure semantics. Changes in precursor lots, instruments, calibration, substrate, chamber history, catalyst aging, processing, or mechanism create distribution shift and negative-transfer risk. Source information therefore needs task/context labels, reference experiments, uncertainty-aware weighting, comparison against target-only baselines, and rejection when it ceases to help. Systematic meta-learning demonstrations across genuinely different chemistries remain scarce. (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000020, pqac-00000041, pqac-00000043, pqac-00000045) | Wakabayashi and Otsuka, [10.48550/arXiv.2608.26016](https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2608.26016); Mallia and Caputo, [10.69709/caic.2026.133382](https://doi.org/10.69709/caic.2026.133382); Bennett et al., [10.1038/s41467-026-74425-x](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-74425-x) |
| Human-in-the-loop and error recovery | **UNSOLVED — human supervision is still a requirement, not an optional fallback** | Unattended campaigns face silent analytical failures, sample mix-ups, sensor drift, reagent degradation, clogs, mechanical faults, unsafe proposals, and ambiguous protocol intent. Future systems need observability, identity checks, anomaly attribution, abstention, safe abortion, checkpoint/restart, self-calibration, automatic recovery, regression testing after updates, and standardized escalation/override rules. Humans must retain control of goals, constraints, stopping rules, high-consequence decisions, and interpretation; LLM/agent reasoning requires audit trails and guardrails. (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000026, pqac-00000028, pqac-00000029, pqac-00000033) | Cheng et al., [10.20944/preprints202608.0273.v1](https://doi.org/10.20944/preprints202608.0273.v1); Hao et al., [10.51847/i178allztd](https://doi.org/10.51847/i178allztd); Lee et al., [10.1039/d5mh01984b](https://doi.org/10.1039/d5mh01984b); Silva et al., [10.2172/3377973](https://doi.org/10.2172/3377973) |

Reported contrasts include an approximately $890,000 LabDroid, approximately $40,000 benchtop NMR, and frugal systems from hundreds to tens of thousands of dollars. “Frugal twins,” open hardware, modular components, shared hubs, and cloud Laboratory-as-a-Service lower entry barriers, but sacrifice fidelity or scope and cloud infrastructure costs are passed to users; geographic and institutional inequity persists. query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'
        >>> 'AREA[Phase]PHASE3'

    Location Search:
        Use SEARCH operator for compound location queries:
        >>> 'cancer AND SEARCH[Location](AREA[LocationCity]Boston AND AREA[LocationState]Massachusetts)'

    Complex Boolean:
        Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses:
        >>> '(cancer OR tumor) AND NOT (EXPANSION[None]pediatric OR AREA[StdAge]CHILD)'

    Date Ranges:
        Use RANGE to specify date ranges with formats like "yyyy-MM" or "yyyy-MM-dd".
        Note that MIN and MAX can be used for open-ended ranges:
        >>> AREA[ResultsFirstPostDate]RANGE[2015-01-01, MAX]

Operators:
    EXPANSION[type]: Controls term expansion
        - None: Exact match only, case and accent sensitive
        - Term: Includes lexical variants (plurals, spellings)
        - Concept: Includes UMLS synonyms
        - Relaxation: Relaxes adjacency requirements (default)
        - Lossy: Allows missing partial terms

    COVERAGE[type]: Controls text matching
        - FullMatch: Must match entire field
        - StartsWith: Must match beginning of field
        - EndsWith: Must match end of field
        - Contains: Must match part of field (default)

    AREA[field]: Specifies field to search
        - See Field Reference for available fields

    SEARCH[type]: Groups field searches
        - Location: Groups location-related fields
        - Study: Groups study-related fields

Usage Notes:
    - All search expressions are implicitly OR expressions
    - Operator precedence (highest to lowest): terms/source operators, NOT/context operators, AND, OR
    - Use quotes for exact phrase matching: "heart attack"
    - Use parentheses for grouping: (heart OR cardiac) AND attack
    - Use backslash to escape operators: \AND
    - Default expansion is EXPANSION[Relaxation]
    - Default coverage is COVERAGE[Contains]

Field Reference:
    High Priority Fields (weight >= 0.8):
        - NCTId (1.0): Trial identifier
        - Acronym (1.0): Study acronym
        - BriefTitle (0.89): Short title
        - OfficialTitle (0.85): Full official title
        - Condition (0.81): Medical condition
        - InterventionName (0.8): Primary intervention name

    Medium Priority Fields (0.5-0.79):

        - StdAge (0.65): Standard age groups
        - Keyword (0.6): Study keywords
        - BriefSummary (0.6): Short description
        - SecondaryOutcomeMeasure (0.5): Secondary outcomes

    Low Priority Fields (< 0.5):
        - DesignPrimaryPurpose (0.3): Primary purpose of study
        - StudyType (0.3)
        - Various descriptive, location, and administrative fields

Supported Enums:
    Phase:
        - EARLY_PHASE1: Early Phase 1
        - PHASE1: Phase 1

        - INTERVENTIONAL: Interventional studies

    PrimaryPurpose:
        - TREATMENT: Treatment
        - PREVENTION: Prevention
