info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

query.description:
Query to search for visual content in the document. If you know the specific
figure/table/formula you are looking for, you can specify it here (e.g. "find me
Figure 3" or "extract the table on page 10"). You can also request based on content
(e.g. "find me all volcano plots of gene X" or "I need the formula for the growth rate").
You can even include explicit instructions for the LLM agent to follow (if helpful, not
necessarily required). The more specific and clear your query is here, the higher the
chance of success.
query.title: Query

text_name.description: Name of a text chunk (e.g., 'smith2023example pages 1-5').
text_name.title: Text Name

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

artifact_type.description:
Artifact type to create. Must be one of: table,
code_block, blockquote, image.
artifact_type.title: Artifact Type

description.description:
Description of what you want in the artifact. Be specific
about what information should be included, how it should be organized,
and what columns/sections/content you want. This guides the summary LLM.
For image type, describe the visual you want generated in detail.
description.title: Description

info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation
history thus far, only the question and each text. Note that it only sees text, no images or other
media from the contents (though tables and formulae may be parseable in some cases).

Think of this tool as an efficient way to deeply scan all retrieved documents for evidence. It
is complementary to the `read_text` tool, which can be used to directly inspect a subset of the
retrieved documents.

A valuable time to invoke this tool is after another tool finds potentially relevant documents.
Feel free to invoke this tool in parallel with other tools, but do not call this tool in parallel with itself.
Only invoke this tool when the document count is above zero, or this tool will be useless.

If you call this tool 2+ times and repeatedly get 'No relevant evidence found',
consider whether the answer might be in visual content (figures/tables) rather than text,
and use appropriate tools if available to access that content.

Once you receive evidence from this tool:

1. Read Carefully: Don't skim. The evidence may contain multiple similar terms
   or values—make sure you identify the RIGHT one.

2. For Comparative Questions: If the question asks "which X has greatest Y",
   check that the evidence includes information about ALL relevant X options, not
   just one or two. If you only see partial information, gather more evidence.

3. Check for Noise: Verify that numbers or terms aren't just metadata
   (page numbers, reference IDs, dates). Look for the value in meaningful
   scientific context.

4. Context Matters: A term appearing 71 times doesn't mean it's always the answer.
   Verify which occurrence actually answers the question asked.

If the evidence doesn't clearly answer the question, gather more evidence before
concluding. Don't guess based on partial information.

question.description: Specific question to gather evidence for.
question.title: Question

text_name_focus_list.description:
if there are known text names that are relevant to the question,
you can specify them here. This will ensure that the tool will look at these text names
first, and then look at the rest of the evidence. If left as `None`, an embedding
search will be performed on underlying content to find most relevant texts.

info.name: update_plan
info.description:
Update the plan for a specific or new objective using a JSON string to create or
replace the existing objective.

The updated_json should be a JSON string representing a single plan objective object.

You may use this tool to update an objective, create a new one, or change
strategy if the current plan is not working. Only change strategy significantly
as a last resort, after trying very hard to make the current plan work.

Only mark an objective as completed if you are absolutely sure that it has been fully
met. If it is only partially met, you may add additional objectives to the plan for
what is missing.

plan_objective_id.description: The id of the objective to update.
plan_objective_id.title: Plan Objective Id

updated_plan_objective_json.description:
A JSON string representing the updated objective.
It should be a dictionary with the with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id matching plan_objective_id, if not found, a new objective is created.
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.

info.name: patent_search
info.description:
Search for patents to increase the patent count.

Repeat previous calls with the same query to continue a search.
Only repeat a maximum of three times.
This tool can be called concurrently.
This tool introduces novel patents, so invoke it when just beginning
or when unsatisfied with the current evidence.

query.description:
A search query for patents (using Google Patents). Never include temporal
filters here (e.g. specific years or dates); instead use the `after` and `before`
arguments. Never include author filters here; instead use the `inventor` argument.
Supports the following syntax, but they can be brittle and are not preferred; try
simple queries where possible:
- Boolean operators: AND (default), OR, and - (NOT)
- Exact phrases: "quoted text"
- Proximity: NEAR/x, ADJ/x (ordered), WITH (20 words), SAME (200 words)
- Field search: TI=(title), AB=(abstract), CL=(claims)
- CPC codes: cpc:A01B or CPC=B60R22/low (includes children)
- Wildcards: ? (0-1 char), * (0+ chars), # (exactly 1 char)
- Chemistry: exact molecule names, SSS=molecule (substructure),
  ~molecule (similar), SMILES strings, SMARTS=pattern, InChI keys,
  CL=~molecule (chemistry in claims)
query.title: Query

after.description:
Minimum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20150101' for patents after Jan 1, 2015.
after.title: After

before.description:
Maximum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20200101' for patents before Jan 1, 2020.
before.title: Before

date_type.description:
Type of date that after and before refer to. Must be either 'publication'
or 'filing'. Only necessary to set if after and/or before are set.

info.name: open_targets_search

Adds new disease-target association data to the state and returns top search results.

disease_names.description:
List of disease names to search for.
Usage:
disease_names = ["Alzheimer's"] ->
    Returns top targets for Alzheimer's
disease_names = ["Alzheimer's", "Diabetes"], target_names = ["PSEN1"] ->
    Filters for only PSEN1-Alzheimer's/Diabetes evidence
disease_names = ["Alzheimer's"], drug_names = ["Aducanumab"] ->
    Filters for Alzheimer's disease-target pairs treated by Aducanumab

Abstract:
<jats:p>Scientific discovery is fundamentally a problem-solving process involving distributed intelligence. Human intuition, computational reasoning, and experimental execution are distributed across people, instruments, and software systems, limiting the speed and scale of discovery. Although automation, high-throughput experimentation, foundation models, and cloud infrastructure have accelerated individual stages of the scientific workflow, they have not unified the discovery process. We hypothesize that the next generation of laboratories will be agentic: environments in which scientists, AI systems, and robotic platforms operate as collaborative discovery partners, with humans contributing the parts of discovery that remain hardest to make explicit: asking the right questions and holding provisional mechanistic models of how a system works. The key missing layer is an agentic harnessing layer that continuously integrates hypothesis, literature-derived evidence, experimental data, uncertainty, and experimental state into a shared “laboratory world model”—a dynamic representation of the scientific system and its evolving context. By maintaining and updating this lab world model, the agentic harnessing layer enables coordinated decision-making, adaptive planning, and increasingly autonomous scientific workflows across humans and machines. A central challenge is that much of the scientific research process remains inaccessible to machines, including tacit knowledge, human observations, adaptive decision-making, and evolving experimental context. Advances in multimodal AI and immersive interfaces may help bridge this gap, allowing humans, agents, and robotic systems to collaborate seamlessly in scientific discovery rather than simply automating isolated tasks. Agentic laboratories could provide a new architecture for science, integrating human, artificial, and physical intelligence into a unified discovery system.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>In iterative optimization, actions are adjusted based on what we see—such as dosing until dissolution or stirring until mixing is complete. Self-driving laboratories (SDLs) offer an opportunity to guide experimental adjustments based on such visual feedback in an autonomous, iterative way. However, current SDLs do not monitor these visual cues. HeinSight 4.0 fills this gap by integrating computer vision into SDLs to enable real-time experimental adjustments based on visual feedback. The computer vision detects equipment (e.g., reactor, vial), classifies chemical phases (solid, liquid, air), and analyzes image features such as turbidity and color. HeinSight 4.0 tracks these physical characteristics frame by frame and interprets physical states (e.g., dissolution, separation). This data feeds into a rule-based system that integrates with the SDL to make real-time experimental adjustments. We demonstrate HeinSight 4.0 adaptability across two pharmaceutical case studies: purification (solubility screening) and drug formulation (melt spray congeal). We also developed a hardware-agnostic architecture and deployed it across two institutions with distinct robotic systems. The open-source HeinSight 4.0 enables SDLs to see, think, and act in real time.</jats:p>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Polymeric materials underpin modern technologies spanning energy storage, microelectronics, healthcare and sustainable manufacturing. Yet their rational design remains exceptionally challenging because material performance emerges from complex interactions among molecular composition, chain architecture, processing history and hierarchical structural evolution across multiple length and time scales. Consequently, polymer research has long relied on labor-intensive experimentation and fragmented modeling approaches, limiting both mechanistic understanding and innovation efficiency. Recent advances in data infrastructure, machine learning, large artificial intelligence (AI) models and laboratory automation are beginning to reshape this landscape. Rather than functioning as isolated tools, polymer databases, predictive models, AI agents and automated laboratories are increasingly converging into interconnected discovery ecosystems. As a result, the central challenge is shifting from improving predictive accuracy alone to enabling reliable decision-making, adaptive learning and seamless integration across computation, experimentation and scientific reasoning. We argue that polymer science is entering an era of autonomous discovery, in which data, simulation, reasoning and experimentation operate within self-improving feedback loops that continuously generate hypotheses, design materials, execute experiments and refine predictive models. By unifying molecular design, process optimization, experimental validation and industrial translation, such autonomous ecosystems establish a more predictive, reproducible and scalable paradigm for polymer innovation, fundamentally transforming how polymer research is conducted.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Halide perovskites (HPs) are emerging as key materials in the fight against global warming with well recognized applications, such as photovoltaics, and emergent opportunities, such as photocatalysis for methane removal and environmental remediation. These current and emergent applications are enabled by a unique combination of high absorption coefficients, tunable band gaps, and long carrier diffusion lengths, making them highly efficient for solar energy conversion. To address the challenge of discovery and optimization of HPs in huge chemical and compositional spaces of possible candidates, this perspective discusses a comprehensive strategy for screening HPs through automated high-throughput and combinatorial synthesis techniques. Our ultimate goal of this work is to transition from laboratory-scale innovations to real-world applications, ensuring that HPs can be deployed effectively in technologies that mitigate global warming, such as in solar energy harvesting and methane removal systems.

Abstract:
<jats:p>The production of green hydrogen through water splitting requires highly efficient electrocatalysts, but the current trial-and-error-based synthesis or discovery is time-consuming, costly and resource-intensive. Machine learning (ML) provides a powerful, data-driven alternative that can model complex structure-activity relationships across large chemical spaces at orders-of-magnitude speed. This review systematically overviews the life cycle of the electrocatalyst research and development application of ML. First, the thermodynamic and kinetic principles of the hydrogen and oxygen evolution reactions are summarised, along with some well-adopted and accepted activity descriptors. Then we explore data sources, featurization approaches, and algorithms, and discuss the model space, from a simple interpretable model to a graph neural network to a generative model, in the context of the ML toolkit. Strategic applications are discussed for high-throughput virtual screening of alloys and single-atom catalysts, as well as multifunctional activity prediction for overall water splitting, and stability optimisation under operating conditions. The topic of emerging frontiers is highlighted, including high-entropy alloys, amorphous materials, and linking atomic-scale understanding to device-level performance through integration with density functional theory. Finally, the problems of data scarcity, model interpretability and the discrepancy between computational predictions and industrial implementation are discussed, along with future directions for closed-loop discovery and self-driving laboratories. Incorporating ML into electrocatalyst design and combining it with autonomous experimentation will revolutionise this process, from simulation to energy solution, dramatically speeding it up.</jats:p>

Abstract:

                    <jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The transition to clean energy demands efficient and scalable electrochemical energy storage (EES) systems, including metal-ion batteries, metal-sulfur batteries, and supercapacitors. Carbon materials are indispensable for EES systems owing to their exceptional electrical conductivity, electrochemical stability, and structural versatility, yet their complex structures complicate structure-property mappings, challenging traditional trial-and-error design paradigms. Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) offer transformative solutions by uncovering hidden structure-property relationships and accelerating material discovery. Although various EES materials have been benefited from this advantage, the study on carbon materials by this new research paradigm is just beginning. This review provides a comprehensive evaluation of AI-assisted methodologies applied to carbon materials across diverse EES devices, including metal-ion batteries, metal-sulfur batteries, and supercapacitors. We systematically summarize the core workflows of ML in materials science, spanning data acquisition, feature engineering, and predictive modeling, while highlighting AI-driven theoretical simulations like ML interatomic potentials. Finally, we outline emerging paradigms and future prospects, emphasizing the integration of large language models (LLMs), active learning to overcome small-data limitations, and the development of autonomous, self-driving laboratories for next-generation carbon electrode design. This review also provides challenges and limitations of applying AI-assisted methodologies in the research of carbon in EES domain.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>The solid-state electrolytes (SSE) are gaining tremendous attention in designing rechargeable batteries with remarkable energy density and safety features for next-generation energy storage device applications. The rational design of SSE with promising ionic conductivity, higher electrochemical stability windows, and stable electrode-electrolyte interfaces remain a formidable challenge, traditionally hindered by trial-and-error experimentation and computationally expensive theoretical simulations. Here, we systematically review the recent breakthroughs in the artificial intelligence (AI)-driven design of SSE, spanning electrochemical stability and ionic conductivity domains, with a particular focus on how machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) are fundamentally transforming the discovery and optimization landscape. We critically discuss the synergy between first-principles density functional theory (DFT), molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, and advanced AI algorithms including supervised and unsupervised learning (SL, UL), graph neural networks (GNNs), and Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials (MLIP) that collectively enable accurate prediction of ionic conductivity, elucidation of ion transport mechanisms, and high-throughput screening (HTS) of vast chemical spaces. Emphasis is placed on descriptor engineering that bridges atomic-level structural features (e.g., lattice parameters, activation energies, defect chemistry) with macroscopic electrochemical performance, as well as the emerging paradigm of closed-loop, self-driving laboratories for autonomous materials discovery. Furthermore, AI-guided strategies have demonstrated remarkable interfacial ionic transport mechanism. Despite these transformative advances, persistent challenges including data scarcity, limited descriptor transferability, discrepancies between theoretical predictions and experimental realization, remain significant challenges. Looking forward, the convergence of AI with high-throughput experimentation and multiscale modeling promises to redefine SSE discovery, accelerating the deployment of high-performance all solid-state batteries (ASSBs) for sustainable energy storage.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Self-driving laboratories (SDLs) promise an accelerated application of the scientific method. Through the automation of experimental workflows, along with autonomous experimental planning, SDLs hold the potential to greatly accelerate research in chemistry and materials discovery. This review provides an in-depth analysis of the state-of-the-art in SDL technology, its applications across various scientific disciplines, and the potential implications for research and industry. This review additionally provides an overview of the enabling technologies for SDLs, including their hardware, software, and integration with laboratory infrastructure. Most importantly, this review explores the diverse range of scientific domains where SDLs have made significant contributions, from drug discovery and materials science to genomics and chemistry. We provide a comprehensive review of existing real-world examples of SDLs, their different levels of automation, and the challenges and limitations associated with each domain.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Discovering new high-performance materials and alloys is often likened to finding a needle in a haystack because the design space of chemical compositions and processing conditions is astronomically large, and the discovery process is laborious and prohibitively costly. This perspective articulates a research agenda for autonomous materials and metallurgy discovery platforms that combine closed-loop machine learning with robotic experimentation and traditional materials engineering precepts to formulate, process, and test candidate materials with reduced human intervention, and to iterate recursively for stepwise optimization. It explores how sequential learning methods, generative modeling, and hybrid model-based strategies can analyze multimodal experimental data and propose new compositions and processing schedules for subsequent experiments. This approach has the potential to considerably accelerate the pace of discoveries, from decades to mere weeks. Representation learning for material formulations, the injection of domain knowledge into decision-making, and the mechatronic design of robotics that can safely execute harsh processing are all explored as essential components in closing the autonomous loop. Surveyed exemplars show order-of-magnitude improvements in experimental throughput and discovery efficiency. Furthermore, the paper proposes a multidimensional framework for classifying and evaluating the autonomy, complexity, and integration levels of self-driving laboratories, intended to give researchers and practitioners a structured approach to benchmarking future developments in the field. The perspective concludes with an analysis of data infrastructure, simulation coupling, robustness, and human-machine collaboration, distilled into a structured research agenda whose pursuit would broaden adoption across energy, aerospace, and other sectors.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The chemical and biochemical sciences are undergoing a profound digital transformation that is giving rise to the emerging paradigm of the digital analytical sciences, driven by an increasing need for research data digitalization, structuring, and standardization. This Trends article provides a bird’s-eye view of how FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) data ecosystems are evolving from administrative guidelines into a critical enabler of modern analytical discovery. Because major advances in artificial intelligence (AI) depend fundamentally on structured and openly accessible scientific data, we discuss how the analytical sciences are now laying the corresponding infrastructural foundations needed to support the next generation of data-driven research. However, in domains such as biophotonics and advanced spectroscopy, large, comprehensively annotated experimental datasets remain limited, and algorithmic advances alone cannot fully compensate for data scarcity or poor standardization. To address this challenge, we examine the rapidly emerging field of physics-informed deep learning, in which physical laws and domain knowledge are incorporated directly into AI pipelines. By leveraging quantum-chemical simulations and transfer-matrix optics to generate synthetic pretraining data, these hybrid approaches can improve the robustness and generalizability of predictive models trained on limited experimental datasets. Finally, we discuss the emerging role of scientific representation learning and argue that realizing the full potential of AI in chemistry will require continued advances in hybrid algorithms alongside a sustained commitment to FAIR data governance and open scientific data infrastructures.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>Large language model (LLM)-based agents can increasingly support and empower human scientists in their work by reading literature, generating hypotheses, designing experiments, analyzing data, interpreting results, and drafting manuscripts. In parallel, robotics and programmable, cloud-connected laboratories have the potential to transform wet-lab operations into software-addressable infrastructure. Yet biological experiments face a persistent reality gap in which silent failures, temporal drift, contamination, sample mix-ups, and ambiguous protocol intent can invalidate an otherwise sound experimental plan. Closing this gap is essential for bringing the speed of modern computational discovery to experimental biology and requires audit-grade execution and verification. Here, we distinguish scripted automation from flexible, AI-enabled autonomy and outline a staged roadmap toward human-led and trustworthy “self-driving” labs for biology. We define laboratory autonomy in the context of a human-led scientific endeavor as a bounded control loop in which scientists set goals and constraints, agents help plan and coordinate experiments, instruments execute experiments and report machine-checkable evidence, and humans verify and interpret results and govern high-consequence decisions. We discuss where such systems are most appropriate and relevant today and where caution or deferral is needed. We map key lab-side potential failure modes and argue for verifiability-first autonomy. If developed responsibly, such systems could enable scientists to more efficiently decipher combinatorially large perturbation, design, and optimization spaces that are currently impractical to test experimentally, while empowering, rather than replacing, human creativity and judgment in experimental biological discovery.</jats:p>

Abstract:
In this work, we highlight the need for dynamic workflow managers in self‐driving laboratories (SDLs) and optimizers for Materials Acceleration Platforms (MAPs). While MAPs leverage artificial intelligence (AI) and automation to accelerate materials discovery, static workflow managers limit scalability, and flexibility. We demonstrate the benefits of modular, adaptable orchestrators by integrating PerQueue, a dynamic workflow manager, into a color‐mixing robot, streamlining task coordination and AI‐driven optimization. Additionally, we assess various MAP‐relevant methodologies based on their maturity and readiness for integration. This assessment underlines the importance of flexible workflow managers in advancing SDLs and optimizers, paving the way for more effective future MAP implementations. Achieving seamless integration requires addressing challenges like ensuring data provenance, adhering to findable, accessible, interoperable, reusable principles, and adapting workflows to changing experimental conditions—key elements for the successful deployment of MAPs.

The development of automated high-throughput experimental platforms has enabled fast sampling of high-dimensional decision spaces. To reach target properties efficiently, these platforms are increasingly paired with intelligent experimental design. However, current optimizers show limitations in maintaining sufficient exploration/exploitation balance for problems dealing with multiple conflicting objectives and complex constraints. Here, we devised an Evolution-Guided Bayesian Optimization (EGBO) algorithm that integrates selection pressure in parallel with a q-Noisy Expected Hypervolume Improvement (qNEHVI) optimizer; this not only solves for the Pareto Front (PF) efficiently but also achieves better coverage of the PF while limiting sampling in the infeasible space. The algorithm was developed together with a custom self-driving lab for seed-mediated silver nanoparticle synthesis, targeting 3 objectives (1) optical properties, (2) fast reaction, and (3) minimal seed usage alongside complex constraints. We demonstrated that, with appropriate constraint handling, EGBO performance improves upon state-of-the-art qNEHVI. Furthermore, across various synthetic multi-objective problems, EGBO showed significative hypervolume improvement, revealing the synergy between selection pressure and the qNEHVI optimizer. We also demonstrated EGBO’s good coverage of the PF as well as comparatively better ability to propose feasible solutions. Experience-driven optimization has been pivotal in advancing organic photovoltaics, where chemically intuitive and stepwise tuning of processing parameters can yield high-performance organic solar cells (OSCs). However, systematically locating optimal regions under high-dimensional, strongly coupled, and multi-objective constraints remains challenging across diverse scenarios. Here, we introduce a closed-loop workflow base on multi-objective Bayesian optimization for efficient process optimization of OSCs. Applied to a quaternary system comprising the widely used polymer donors PM6 and D18 and the non-fullerene acceptors BTP-eC9 and L8BO, the workflow navigates an eight-dimensional space jointly defined by composition and fabrication variables, encompassing 2.2 × 10 14 possible combinations. Within five active-learning cycles, the search rapidly converges to a high-performance region, achieving a power conversion efficiency exceeding 20% while drastically reducing the time and effort compared to conventional trial-and-error approaches. The generalizability of the workflow is further demonstrated across different material systems and fabrication methods, consistently guiding the optimization toward high-performance regions in only a few iterations. This work establishes a generalizable, efficient, and scalable closed-loop framework for the rapid identification of optimal process windows in high-dimensional, multi-objective systems for organic photovoltaics and beyond.

laboratories, transformative systems designed to overcome limitations in traditional experimental approaches. This review

systems to optimize experimental workflows, reduce human intervention, and enhance efficiency in complex reaction
environments. Key developments include AI-driven reaction pathway planning, closed-loop optimization frameworks, and robotic
platforms capable of executing multi-step synthesis with minimal expert oversight. Leading research groups have demonstrated

                  <jats:p>Hydrogen storage remains a central bottleneck for scalable hydrogen energy systems due to the multiscale and coupled nature of the thermodynamics, kinetics, and microstructural evolution of hydrogen storage materials (HSMs). Although artificial intelligence (AI) has accelerated materials discovery, current approaches remain constrained by fragmented data, limited physical consistency, and weak integration with experimental validation. Here, we propose a unified framework that integrates coherent data infrastructure, physics-grounded modeling, and AI-driven inverse design within a closed-loop discovery paradigm. By constraining optimization with thermodynamics, kinetics, uncertainty, provenance, and experimental feedback, this approach enables adaptive, physically consistent optimization, thereby establishing a pathway toward autonomous, digital-twin-enabled discovery of HSMs.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>Low-cost self-driving labs (SDLs) offer faster prototyping, low-risk hands-on experience, and a test bed for sophisticated experimental planning software which helps us develop state-of-the-art SDLs.</jats:p>

Relevant Snippet:
This review proposes the concept of a “frugal twin,” similar to a digital twin, but for physical experiments. Frugal twins range from simple toy examples to low-cost surrogates of high-cost research systems. For example, a color-mixing self-driving laboratory (SDL) can serve as a low-cost version of a costly multi-step chemical discovery SDL. Frugal twins already provide hands-on experience for SDLs with low costs and low risks. They can also offer as test beds for software prototyping (e.g., optimization, data infrastructure), and a low barrier to entry for democratizing SDLs. However, there is room for improvement. The true value of frugal twins can be realized in three core areas. Firstly, hardware and software modularity; secondly, purpose-built design (human-inspired vs. hardware-centric vs. human-in-the-loop); and thirdly state-of-the-art (SOTA) software (e.g., multi-fidelity optimization). We also describe the ethical benefits and risks that come with the democratization of science through frugal twins. For future work, we suggest ideas for new frugal twins, SDL educational course outcomes, and a classification scheme for autonomy levels.

By integrating active and deep learning algorithms with multi-level datasets ranging from quantum mechanical simulations to high-throughput flow-based experiments, these platforms establish closed-loop frameworks that guide complex nanofabrication processes in real time. Such AI-driven systems lower material and energy consumption, enable the precise design of nanostructures with tailored optical, electronic, and mechanical properties, and create research opportunities that were previously difficult to realize. Abstract:
<jats:p>The discovery of next-generation battery electrolytes increasingly involves complex, multicomponent formulations that demand high-throughput, systematic exploration. We present the Bayesian Robotic Investigator of Novel Electrolytes (BRINE), a cost-effective, self-driving laboratory (SDL) that autonomously prepares and tests mixed electrolyte solutions. BRINE combines an open-source liquid-handling robot with a potentiostat and custom-made electrodes to mix reagents and perform electrochemical measurements without human intervention. A Bayesian optimization routine navigates multidimensional composition spaces, allowing the platform to rapidly identify promising formulations. As a proof of concept, BRINE mapped ionic conductivity in two aqueous electrolyte spaces (i) aqueous mixtures of NaCl, KCl, MgCl2, and CaCl2, and (ii) battery-oriented mixtures containing ZnCl2, KCl, NH4Cl, NaCl, and EMIMCl, testing ~230 unique compositions in under 18 hours and finding conductivities up to 32.13 S/m. These results demonstrate how closed-loop autonomous experimentation and optimization accelerate the identification of electrolytes with the highest conductivity across a large multicomponent composition space, while minimizing experimental variability. This work lays the foundation for broader electrochemical studies using the BRINE platform.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>Chemical-enhanced oil recovery (EOR) is a field of study that can gain significantly from artificial intelligence (AI), addressing uncertainties such as mobility control, interfacial tension reduction, wettability alteration, and emulsifications. The primary objective of this paper is to introduce an integrated framework for AI and chemical EOR for energy harvest operations. Central emphasis is placed on the energy transition, with the aim of expediting the development of cleaner energy harvesting systems and attaining the goal of net-zero emission. To do so, we present how the energy transition is changing the manufacturing of the chemicals for EOR application. For this, the uncertainty associated with materials' design and critical role of the simulators for transferring the laboratory experiences into full-field implementations is discussed. The concept of digitalization and its impact on energy companies are highlighted. The role of digital twin in simulators integration is discussed, emphasizing how increased data access can help design more tolerant chemicals for harsh reservoir environments using real-time data. Also, we discuss how the chemical suppliers, research institutes, startups, and field operators can benefit from self-leaning and robotic laboratories for chemicals manufacturing. Moreover, this paper explores how including AI perspectives can improve our understanding of developing chemical formulations by blending hybrid capabilities. This approach contributes to making energy production more sustainable and aligning with the goal of zero emissions. A workflow is presented to demonstrate how the integration of AI and chemical EOR can be used for both hydrocarbon production and other energy transition operations, such as carbon capture, utilization and storage, hydrogen storage, and geothermal reservoirs. The outcome of this paper stands as a pioneering effort that uniquely addresses these challenges for both academia and the industry and can open many additional doors and identify topics requiring further investigations.

The excerpt frames multimodal characterization as a major departure from single-objective, black-box Bayesian optimization. XRD, spectroscopy, microscopy, and electrochemistry can produce heterogeneous, partially observable, noisy, delayed, or missing measurements, while each modality may describe a different aspect of material quality. Consequently, closing the loop requires defining and reconciling multiple potentially competing objectives rather than reducing experiments to one scalar score. The workflow must also account for failed syntheses, feasibility constraints, mixed variable types, variable measurement cost, and asynchronous data acquisition. These issues make the standard Gaussian-process plus expected-improvement recipe insufficient and motivate models and acquisition strategies that can represent multimodal observations, trade-offs, uncertainty, and practical experiment costs. For multi-fidelity BO, the stated challenges are that measurements may differ in cost, accuracy, availability, and delay; the optimizer must decide when inexpensive or lower-fidelity characterization is informative enough and when expensive high-fidelity measurements are justified. Transfer learning across chemical systems is similarly nontrivial: historical data from related materials, substrates, instruments, or material families may enable warm starts or transferred priors, but differences between systems can produce nonstationarity and misleading knowledge transfer. The excerpt identifies these as design problems but does not provide specific algorithms or quantitative solutions.

4. Shortage of negative results - UNSOLVED. Chemical databases emphasize successes; failed experiments not routinely captured or published; essential for model training and avoiding bias (Gauthier et al. 10.1039/d5dd00297d; Hao et al. 10.51847/i178allztd)
5. Closing the loop with multiple orthogonal characterization modalities - UNSOLVED. Most SDLs optimize a single scalar; integrating XRD, spectroscopy, microscopy, electrochemistry requires data fusion, uncertainty calibration, and decision models; missing/incomplete data across modalities (Wakabayashi & Otsuka 10.48550/arxiv.2608.26016; Foadian et al. 10.1021/acsmaterialsau.4c00096; Müller et al. 10.48550/arxiv.2609.04564)
6. Multi-fidelity and multi-objective optimization - UNSOLVED. Low-fidelity measurements may be weakly correlated or biased; Pareto-front acquisition is complex; scalarization compresses trade-offs; cost-aware acquisition functions needed (Wakabayashi & Otsuka 10.48550/arxiv.2608.26016; Hippalgaonkar et al. 10.21203/rs.3.rs-3578558/v1)
7. Transfer/meta-learning across chemistries - UNSOLVED. Negative transfer risk when source/target systems differ; experimental drift, batch effects, instrument differences; warm starts require compatible inputs/objectives; few systematic demonstrations (Wakabayashi & Otsuka 10.48550/arxiv.2608.26016; Mallia & Caputo 10.69709/caic.2026.133382; Bennett et al. 10.1038/s41467-026-74425-x)
8. Human-in-the-loop and error recovery - UNSOLVED. Silent failures, sensor drift, reagent degradation; no standardized escalation or recovery protocols; human oversight needed for goals, constraints, safety; LLM agents can hallucinate or make unsafe proposals (Cheng et al. 10.20944/preprints202608.0273.v1; Hao et al. 10.51847/i178allztd; Lee et al. 10.1039/d5mh01984b)
9. Cost/accessibility - UNSOLVED. Multi-million dollar/euro investments concentrated in elite institutions; frugal twins from ~$100-$30,000 proposed but limited capability; cloud labs help but have infrastructure costs; global equity gap (Lo et al. 10.1039/d3dd00223c; Mallia & Caputo 10.69709/caic.2026.133382; Jiang et al. 10.4208/cicc.2025.90.03)"}

{"answer": "# Open Problems and Future Directions for Self-Driving Laboratories in Materials Chemistry and Electrochemistry (2023–2026)

## Overview

A systematic survey of recent reviews, perspectives, and roadmap papers (2023–2026) reveals a clear consensus: while self-driving laboratories (SDLs) have demonstrated impressive domain-specific capabilities—from nanoparticle synthesis to electrocatalyst screening—the transition from narrow, single-loop demonstrations to general-purpose, networked, trustworthy autonomous discovery platforms remains incomplete. The SDL 2.0 vision articulated by Lee et al. (DOI: 10.1039/d5mh01984b) defines six pillars—interoperability, collaboration, generalizability, orchestration, safety, and creativity—all of which remain aspirational rather than realized (pqac-00000033, pqac-00000034). The comprehensive Chemical Reviews survey by Tom et al. (DOI: 10.1021/acs.chemrev.4c00055) and the Trustworthy Autonomous Science roadmap by Silva et al. (DOI: 10.2172/3377973) further confirm that the field has not yet achieved end-to-end, experimentally self-validating autonomous discovery (pqac-00000007, pqac-00000011, pqac-00000048).

Below, the nine concrete named challenges are assessed individually. **All nine remain unsolved as of 2026**, although each has seen partial progress.

The following table provides a compact reference for each challenge, its 2026 status, specific unresolved technical issues, and supporting references with DOIs:

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

## 1. Orchestration and Interoperability Standards (SiLA2, LabOP, AnIML, Bluesky, Chemputer/XDL)

**Status: UNSOLVED.** No universally adopted standard spans instruments, workflow descriptions, analytical formats, and orchestration layers. Tom et al. identify the absence of standardized APIs from instrument manufacturers as a fundamental bottleneck, presenting SiLA2 as a promising device-communication protocol modeled on ROS but requiring much broader adoption (pqac-00000011). Lee et al. recommend SiLA and OPC UA for standardized interfaces alongside modular, open-source orchestration software, while acknowledging that hardware-specific communication protocols, absence of shared digital infrastructure, and lack of common calibration benchmarks continue to impede scalability and reproducibility (pqac-00000033, pqac-00000037). Steensen et al. (DOI: 10.1002/aidi.202500067) document that materials-science ontologies remain immature and that semantic data integration has in practice been post hoc rather than built into live campaigns (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000014). Jiang et al. (DOI: 10.4208/cicc.2025.90.03) specifically call for universal communication protocols such as SiLA2 and AnIML to standardize cross-platform compatibility (pqac-00000005). Critically, syntactic portability of a protocol file does not guarantee chemically equivalent execution across heterogeneous platforms—a point emphasized as a fundamental reproducibility risk (pqac-00000006).

## 2. FAIR Data and Metadata Capture

**Status: UNSOLVED.** Data remain fragmented across bespoke instrument-specific files and laboratory-specific schemas. Gauthier et al. (DOI: 10.1039/d5dd00297d) demonstrate a FAIR research data infrastructure for the Swiss Cat+ platform using Matryoshka files, ontology-driven metadata modeling, ASM-JSON analytical outputs, RDF/Turtle conversion, and SHACL validation—but this remains a single-site exemplar rather than a community standard (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000012, pqac-00000015). Tali et al. (DOI: 10.1039/d5dd00175g) present SEARS, a cloud-native platform for multi-lab FAIR data, but similarly serve as a proof of concept. Hao et al. (DOI: 10.51847/i178allztd) emphasize that a reusable experimental record must bind raw analytical traces to reagent identities, batch IDs, preparation history, environment, calibration state, software/model versions, branching decisions, manual interventions, and failures—metadata that current SDL records routinely omit (pqac-00000000). Steensen et al. confirm that ontologized data integration into optimization campaigns has not been achieved systematically (pqac-00000010).

## 3. Reproducibility and Round-Robin Benchmarking Between Labs

**Status: UNSOLVED.** No accepted multi-lab round-robin protocol for SDLs exists. Hao et al. call for prospective challenge sets involving noise, constraints, missing measurements, failed runs, distributional change, and long-duration campaigns that reveal instrument drift, reagent degradation, software changes, and maintenance burdens—none of which have been standardized (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000002, pqac-00000027). Silva et al. (DOI: 10.2172/3377973) highlight that LLM-based orchestration is nondeterministic, making run-to-run reproducibility difficult, and that verification infrastructure has not kept pace with agent capabilities; they recommend end-to-end reproduction benchmarks, uncertainty quantification, and full provenance recording of prompts, responses, decisions, data, tools, and model versions (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000030). Mallia and Caputo (DOI: 10.69709/caic.2026.133382) propose cross-platform transfer benchmarks and reference datasets for stress-testing candidate schemas, but note that poisoning-resistant model-exchange protocols and formal inter-lab protocols remain absent (pqac-00000024). Lee et al. call for reference experiments and calibration materials but do not describe established round-robin procedures (pqac-00000032).

## 4. Shortage of Negative Results

**Status: UNSOLVED.** Chemical datasets disproportionately retain successful outcomes. Gauthier et al. explicitly note that chemical datasets emphasize successes while omitting failed experiments, and their infrastructure is designed to capture both raw data and metadata for every experimental step including failures (pqac-00000012). Hao et al. emphasize that failed or negative experiments must be interpretable and systematically captured, distinguishing genuine null chemistry from analytical or robotic failure—an important distinction that current systems rarely make (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000004, pqac-00000006). The SDL community has not established incentive structures, data formats, or publication venues that routinely encourage sharing of negative autonomous-experiment outcomes, despite their importance for model training and avoiding selection bias.

## 5. Closing the Loop with Multiple Orthogonal Characterization Modalities

**Status: UNSOLVED.** Most operational SDLs optimize a single scalar objective (e.g., photoluminescence peak, conductivity, yield). Wakabayashi and Otsuka (DOI: 10.48550/arXiv.2608.26016) frame multimodal characterization—XRD, spectroscopy, microscopy, electrochemistry, process logs—as a major open problem requiring data fusion, uncertainty calibration, and decision models that can handle heterogeneous noise, cost, delay, scale, and missingness across modalities (pqac-00000040, pqac-00000041). Müller et al. (DOI: 10.48550/arXiv.2609.04564) demonstrate this concretely: a zero-yield result was ambiguous until the agent accessed raw NMR records, reconstructed the chemical-shift axis, and distinguished a real absence of product from an analytical failure—illustrating that scalar optimization collapses the evidence needed for diagnosis (pqac-00000016). Foadian et al. (DOI: 10.1021/acsmaterialsau.4c00096) emphasize that closing the characterization loop requires identifying rapid, reliable proxy signals that connect high-dimensional measurements to material compositions and functionalities (pqac-00000042). Hao et al. note that molecular plausibility, synthesis, assay activity, mechanism, cellular relevance, and stability are successive but non-equivalent evidence layers that a single scalar objective cannot represent (pqac-00000019).

## 6. Multi-Fidelity and Multi-Objective Optimization

**Status: UNSOLVED.** Wakabayashi and Otsuka provide the most detailed treatment, identifying that low-fidelity measurements are valuable only when sufficiently correlated with the high-fidelity target and inexpensive relative to the information they provide; weak correlation or systematic bias can waste the experimental budget (pqac-00000022). Acquisition functions must jointly balance expected improvement against source-specific costs and determine when further low-fidelity sampling is no longer worthwhile. For multi-objective campaigns, Pareto hypervolume methods become costly, scalarization can compress trade-offs, and batch methods must handle conflicting properties, feasibility constraints, and asynchronous execution (pqac-00000018, pqac-00000020). Hippalgaonkar et al. (DOI: 10.21203/rs.3.rs-3578558/v1) developed EGBO specifically to handle constrained multi-objective problems in SDLs, confirming that standard acquisition functions are insufficient. The battery domain adds long cycling times and substantial cell-to-cell variability, making exhaustive exploration impractical (pqac-00000044, pqac-00000046).

## 7. Transfer/Meta-Learning Across Chemistries

**Status: UNSOLVED.** Transfer is promising within closely related campaigns (e.g., across precursor batches for quantum-dot synthesis, yielding at least twofold acceleration) but unproven across genuinely different chemical systems (pqac-00000021, pqac-00000047). Wakabayashi and Otsuka warn that negative transfer is a realistic risk when source and target systems differ in descriptors, objectives, scales, or failure semantics (pqac-00000043, pqac-00000045). Experimental drift—source depletion, chamber evolution, catalyst aging, batch replacement, calibration changes—can make nominally comparable measurements non-transferable, requiring time-, state-, or change-point-aware surrogate models and reference experiments to assess whether historical data remain reusable (pqac-00000041). Mallia and Caputo identify the cold-start problem and platform specialization as fundamental barriers, proposing foundation models and transfer learning as solutions subject to data-poisoning risks (pqac-00000001). Bennett et al. (DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-74425-x) note that transfer learning and descriptor-based approaches represent future directions for their autonomous catalysis platform (pqac-00000017). Systematic meta-learning demonstrations across genuinely different chemistries remain scarce.

## 8. Human-in-the-Loop and Error Recovery

**Status: UNSOLVED.** Cheng et al. (DOI: 10.20944/preprints202608.0273.v1) provide the most detailed treatment, arguing that autonomous systems must handle silent execution failures, instrument drift, biological variability, sample mix-ups, incomplete troubleshooting, and discrepancies between protocol intent and actual execution (pqac-00000026, pqac-00000028). They call for continuous verification, observability, provenance logs, quality-control artifacts, anomaly feedback, recovery mechanisms, abstention, and escalation to human judgment. **Status: UNSOLVED.** Data remain fragmented across bespoke instrument-specific files and laboratory-specific schemas. Gauthier et al. Steensen et al. confirm that ontologized data integration into optimization campaigns has not been achieved systematically (pqac-00000010).

## 3. Reproducibility and Round-Robin Benchmarking Between Labs

**Status: UNSOLVED.** No accepted multi-lab round-robin protocol for SDLs exists. Silva et al. **Status: UNSOLVED.** Chemical datasets disproportionately retain successful outcomes. Hao et al. emphasize that failed or negative experiments must be interpretable and systematically captured, distinguishing genuine null chemistry from analytical or robotic failure—an important distinction that current systems rarely make (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000004, pqac-00000006). The SDL community has not established incentive structures, data formats, or publication venues that routinely encourage sharing of negative autonomous-experiment outcomes, despite their importance for model training and avoiding selection bias.

**Status: UNSOLVED.** Most operational SDLs optimize a single scalar objective (e.g., photoluminescence peak, conductivity, yield). Hao et al. note that molecular plausibility, synthesis, assay activity, mechanism, cellular relevance, and stability are successive but non-equivalent evidence layers that a single scalar objective cannot represent (pqac-00000019).

**Status: UNSOLVED.** Wakabayashi and Otsuka provide the most detailed treatment, identifying that low-fidelity measurements are valuable only when sufficiently correlated with the high-fidelity target and inexpensive relative to the information they provide; weak correlation or systematic bias can waste the experimental budget (pqac-00000022). All nine remain unsolved, although several have partial standards, prototype infrastructures, or domain-specific demonstrations.*

## 1. Orchestration and Interoperability Standards (SiLA2, LabOP, AnIML, Bluesky, Chemputer/XDL)

**Status: UNSOLVED.** No universally adopted standard spans instruments, workflow descriptions, analytical formats, and orchestration layers. Tom et al. identify the absence of standardized APIs from instrument manufacturers as a fundamental bottleneck, presenting SiLA2 as a promising device-communication protocol modeled on ROS but requiring much broader adoption (tom2024selfdrivinglaboratoriesfor pages 7-8). Lee et al. recommend SiLA and OPC UA for standardized interfaces alongside modular, open-source orchestration software, while acknowledging that hardware-specific communication protocols, absence of shared digital infrastructure, and lack of common calibration benchmarks continue to impede scalability and reproducibility (lee2026towardselfdrivinglaboratory pages 17-19, lee2026towardselfdrivinglaboratory pages 20-21). Steensen et al. (DOI: 10.1002/aidi.202500067) document that materials-science ontologies remain immature and that semantic data integration has in practice been post hoc rather than built into live campaigns (steensen2026thenecessityof pages 3-3, steensen2026thenecessityof pages 2-3). Jiang et al. (DOI: 10.4208/cicc.2025.90.03) specifically call for universal communication protocols such as SiLA2 and AnIML to standardize cross-platform compatibility (jiang2025recentprogressin pages 11-12). Critically, syntactic portability of a protocol file does not guarantee chemically equivalent execution across heterogeneous platforms—a point emphasized as a fundamental reproducibility risk (hao2026doselfdrivinglaboratories pages 4-5).

## 2. FAIR Data and Metadata Capture

**Status: UNSOLVED.** Data remain fragmented across bespoke instrument-specific files and laboratory-specific schemas. Gauthier et al. (DOI: 10.1039/d5dd00297d) demonstrate a FAIR research data infrastructure for the Swiss Cat+ platform using Matryoshka files, ontology-driven metadata modeling, ASM-JSON analytical outputs, RDF/Turtle conversion, and SHACL validation—but this remains a single-site exemplar rather than a community standard (gauthier2025afairresearch pages 3-5, gauthier2025afairresearch pages 1-2, gauthier2025afairresearch pages 2-3). Tali et al. (DOI: 10.1039/d5dd00175g) present SEARS, a cloud-native platform for multi-lab FAIR data, but similarly serve as a proof of concept. Hao et al. (DOI: 10.51847/i178allztd) emphasize that a reusable experimental record must bind raw analytical traces to reagent identities, batch IDs, preparation history, environment, calibration state, software/model versions, branching decisions, manual interventions, and failures—metadata that current SDL records routinely omit (hao2026doselfdrivinglaboratories pages 6-8). Steensen et al. confirm that ontologized data integration into optimization campaigns has not been achieved systematically (steensen2026thenecessityof pages 3-3).

## 3. Reproducibility and Round-Robin Benchmarking Between Labs

**Status: UNSOLVED.** No accepted multi-lab round-robin protocol for SDLs exists. Hao et al. call for prospective challenge sets involving noise, constraints, missing measurements, failed runs, distributional change, and long-duration campaigns that reveal instrument drift, reagent degradation, software changes, and maintenance burdens—none of which have been standardized (hao2026doselfdrivinglaboratories pages 6-8, hao2026doselfdrivinglaboratories pages 8-10, hao2026doselfdrivinglaboratories pages 8-8). Silva et al. (DOI: 10.2172/3377973) highlight that LLM-based orchestration is nondeterministic, making run-to-run reproducibility difficult, and that verification infrastructure has not kept pace with agent capabilities; they recommend end-to-end reproduction benchmarks, uncertainty quantification, and full provenance recording of prompts, responses, decisions, data, tools, and model versions (silva2026towardtrustworthyautonomous pages 17-18, silva2026towardtrustworthyautonomous pages 15-17). Mallia and Caputo (DOI: 10.69709/caic.2026.133382) propose cross-platform transfer benchmarks and reference datasets for stress-testing candidate schemas, but note that poisoning-resistant model-exchange protocols and formal inter-lab protocols remain absent (mallia2026aiguidedselfdrivinglaboratories pages 22-27). Lee et al. call for reference experiments and calibration materials but do not describe established round-robin procedures (lee2026towardselfdrivinglaboratory pages 19-20).

## 4. Shortage of Negative Results

**Status: UNSOLVED.** Chemical datasets disproportionately retain successful outcomes. Gauthier et al. explicitly note that chemical datasets emphasize successes while omitting failed experiments, and their infrastructure is designed to capture both raw data and metadata for every experimental step including failures (gauthier2025afairresearch pages 1-2). Hao et al. emphasize that failed or negative experiments must be interpretable and systematically captured, distinguishing genuine null chemistry from analytical or robotic failure—an important distinction that current systems rarely make (hao2026doselfdrivinglaboratories pages 6-8, hao2026doselfdrivinglaboratories pages 8-8, hao2026doselfdrivinglaboratories pages 4-5). The SDL community has not established incentive structures, data formats, or publication venues that routinely encourage sharing of negative autonomous-experiment outcomes, despite their importance for model training and avoiding selection bias.

## 5. Closing the Loop with Multiple Orthogonal Characterization Modalities

**Status: UNSOLVED.** Most operational SDLs optimize a single scalar objective (e.g., photoluminescence peak, conductivity, yield). Wakabayashi and Otsuka (DOI: 10.48550/arXiv.2608.26016) frame multimodal characterization—XRD, spectroscopy, microscopy, electrochemistry, process logs—as a major open problem requiring data fusion, uncertainty calibration, and decision models that can handle heterogeneous noise, cost, delay, scale, and missingness across modalities (wakabayashi2608bayesianoptimizationfor pages 1-3, wakabayashi2608bayesianoptimizationfor pages 45-48). Müller et al. (DOI: 10.48550/arXiv.2609.04564) demonstrate this concretely: a zero-yield result was ambiguous until the agent accessed raw NMR records, reconstructed the chemical-shift axis, and distinguished a real absence of product from an analytical failure—illustrating that scalar optimization collapses the evidence needed for diagnosis (muller2026laagente\optimatowards pages 11-13). Foadian et al. (DOI: 10.1021/acsmaterialsau.4c00096) emphasize that closing the characterization loop requires identifying rapid, reliable proxy signals that connect high-dimensional measurements to material compositions and functionalities (foadian2024fromsunlightto pages 8-9). Hao et al. note that molecular plausibility, synthesis, assay activity, mechanism, cellular relevance, and stability are successive but non-equivalent evidence layers that a single scalar objective cannot represent (hao2026doselfdrivinglaboratories pages 8-8).

## 6. Multi-Fidelity and Multi-Objective Optimization

**Status: UNSOLVED.** Wakabayashi and Otsuka provide the most detailed treatment, identifying that low-fidelity measurements are valuable only when sufficiently correlated with the high-fidelity target and inexpensive relative to the information they provide; weak correlation or systematic bias can waste the experimental budget (wakabayashi2608bayesianoptimizationfor pages 26-28). Acquisition functions must jointly balance expected improvement against source-specific costs and determine when further low-fidelity sampling is no longer worthwhile. For multi-objective campaigns, Pareto hypervolume methods become costly, scalarization can compress trade-offs, and batch methods must handle conflicting properties, feasibility constraints, and asynchronous execution (wakabayashi2608bayesianoptimizationfor pages 16-17, wakabayashi2608bayesianoptimizationfor pages 1-3). Hippalgaonkar et al. (DOI: 10.21203/rs.3.rs-3578558/v1) developed EGBO specifically to handle constrained multi-objective problems in SDLs, confirming that standard acquisition functions are insufficient. The battery domain adds long cycling times and substantial cell-to-cell variability, making exhaustive exploration impractical (wakabayashi2608bayesianoptimizationfor pages 40-42, wakabayashi2608bayesianoptimizationfor pages 42-44).

## 7. Transfer/Meta-Learning Across Chemistries

**Status: UNSOLVED.** Transfer is promising within closely related campaigns (e.g., across precursor batches for quantum-dot synthesis, yielding at least twofold acceleration) but unproven across genuinely different chemical systems (hao2025autonomousmaterialssynthesis pages 53-56). Wakabayashi and Otsuka warn that negative transfer is a realistic risk when source and target systems differ in descriptors, objectives, scales, or failure semantics (wakabayashi2608bayesianoptimizationfor pages 33-36, wakabayashi2608bayesianoptimizationfor pages 31-33). Experimental drift—source depletion, chamber evolution, catalyst aging, batch replacement, calibration changes—can make nominally comparable measurements non-transferable, requiring time-, state-, or change-point-aware surrogate models and reference experiments to assess whether historical data remain reusable (wakabayashi2608bayesianoptimizationfor pages 45-48). Mallia and Caputo identify the cold-start problem and platform specialization as fundamental barriers, proposing foundation models and transfer learning as solutions subject to data-poisoning risks (mallia2026aiguidedselfdrivinglaboratories pages 17-22). Bennett et al. (DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-74425-x) note that transfer learning and descriptor-based approaches represent future directions for their autonomous catalysis platform (muller2026laagente\optimatowards pages 9-11). Systematic meta-learning demonstrations across genuinely different chemistries remain scarce.

## 8. Human-in-the-Loop and Error Recovery

**Status: UNSOLVED.** Cheng et al. (DOI: 10.20944/preprints202608.0273.v1) provide the most detailed treatment, arguing that autonomous systems must handle silent execution failures, instrument drift, biological variability, sample mix-ups, incomplete troubleshooting, and discrepancies between protocol intent and actual execution (cheng2026towardshumanledagentdriven pages 7-8, cheng2026towardshumanledagentdriven pages 8-11). They call for continuous verification, observability, provenance logs, quality-control artifacts, anomaly feedback, recovery mechanisms, abstention, and escalation to human judgment. Hao et al. emphasize that platforms may lack the perception and adaptability required for unfamiliar samples and failure states, and that co-design must establish admissible actions, stopping rules, and escalation pathways before autonomous operation begins (hao2026doselfdrivinglaboratories pages 6-8, hao2026doselfdrivinglaboratories pages 8-8). Lee et al. note that SDL safety requires contextual hazard detection, predictive diagnostics, automatic recovery, safety-aware planning, and real-time mitigation for unattended operation—capabilities beyond simple threshold alarms (lee2026towardselfdrivinglaboratory pages 17-19). Silva et al. frame reliable human override, screening, auditing, and independent measurements as essential research concerns, noting that agents perform near or below chance on some reproducibility benchmarks (silva2026towardtrustworthyautonomous pages 17-18, silva2026towardtrustworthyautonomous pages 15-17).

## 9. Cost and Accessibility

**Status: UNSOLVED.** Cost remains a decisive barrier to broad adoption. Lo et al. (DOI: 10.1039/d3dd00223c) document the full range: from frugal-twin setups at ~$50–$450 (e.g., MIK-I at ~$450, Jubilee at ~$2,000) to research-grade platforms at $10,000–$30,000, up to industrial systems like the Maholo LabDroid at ~$890,000 (lo2024reviewoflowcost pages 22-23, lo2024reviewoflowcost pages 5-6, lo2024reviewoflowcost pages 6-7, lo2024reviewoflowcost pages 10-11, lo2024reviewoflowcost pages 4-5). A benchtop NMR alone costs ~$40,000, and robust low-cost alternatives to NMR or HPLC-MS under $10,000 do not currently exist (lo2024reviewoflowcost pages 6-7). Mallia and Caputo describe current SDLs as requiring multi-million-euro bespoke investments concentrated in elite institutions, and propose Laboratory-as-a-Service, cloud access, secure tele-operation, standardized experiment descriptions, metered pricing, and open-source hardware to broaden equitable access (mallia2026aiguidedselfdrivinglaboratories pages 22-27). Jiang et al. recommend decentralized resource-sharing, cloud simulation, and shared equipment hubs to reduce capital and operating costs for smaller institutions (jiang2025recentprogressin pages 11-12). Lo et al. emphasize that affordability is context-dependent: prices considered low-cost in developed countries may be unaffordable in the Global South due to limited funding, delivery expenses, and foreign-exchange difficulties (lo2024reviewoflowcost pages 4-5). Multi-fidelity strategies—where inexpensive frugal-twin SDLs explore the parameter space before costly high-fidelity systems refine promising regions—are proposed as a practical cost-reduction mechanism (lo2024reviewoflowcost pages 17-18).

## Conclusion: All Nine Challenges Remain Unsolved

Based on this survey of 15+ recent reviews, perspectives, and roadmap papers, **all nine named challenges remain open problems as of 2026**. None is described as fully resolved by any source consulted. Partial progress includes: SiLA2 and OPC UA gaining adoption as device-level protocols; Matryoshka files and SEARS as FAIR-data exemplars; EGBO and related algorithms for constrained multi-objective optimization; within-campaign transfer learning for nanocrystal synthesis; HeinSight 4.0 for vision-guided error detection; and frugal-twin systems for democratized prototyping and education. However, the gap between these individual advances and the integrated, interoperable, reproducible, accessible, and trustworthy SDL 2.0 envisioned by the community remains substantial.
