*Table: The table maps nine concrete self-driving-laboratory challenges in materials chemistry and electrochemistry to their 2026 status, technical bottlenecks, and supporting DOI-linked sources. All nine remain unsolved, although several have partial standards, prototype infrastructures, or domain-specific demonstrations.*

## 1. Orchestration and Interoperability Standards (SiLA2, LabOP, AnIML, Bluesky, Chemputer/XDL)

**Status: UNSOLVED.** No universally adopted standard spans instruments, workflow descriptions, analytical formats, and orchestration layers. Tom et al. identify the absence of standardized APIs from instrument manufacturers as a fundamental bottleneck, presenting SiLA2 as a promising device-communication protocol modeled on ROS but requiring much broader adoption (pqac-00000011). Lee et al. recommend SiLA and OPC UA for standardized interfaces alongside modular, open-source orchestration software, while acknowledging that hardware-specific communication protocols, absence of shared digital infrastructure, and lack of common calibration benchmarks continue to impede scalability and reproducibility (pqac-00000033, pqac-00000037). Steensen et al. (DOI: 10.1002/aidi.202500067) document that materials-science ontologies remain immature and that semantic data integration has in practice been post hoc rather than built into live campaigns (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000014). Jiang et al. (DOI: 10.4208/cicc.2025.90.03) specifically call for universal communication protocols such as SiLA2 and AnIML to standardize cross-platform compatibility (pqac-00000005). Critically, syntactic portability of a protocol file does not guarantee chemically equivalent execution across heterogeneous platforms—a point emphasized as a fundamental reproducibility risk (pqac-00000006).

## 2. FAIR Data and Metadata Capture

**Status: UNSOLVED.** Data remain fragmented across bespoke instrument-specific files and laboratory-specific schemas. Gauthier et al. (DOI: 10.1039/d5dd00297d) demonstrate a FAIR research data infrastructure for the Swiss Cat+ platform using Matryoshka files, ontology-driven metadata modeling, ASM-JSON analytical outputs, RDF/Turtle conversion, and SHACL validation—but this remains a single-site exemplar rather than a community standard (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000012, pqac-00000015). Tali et al. (DOI: 10.1039/d5dd00175g) present SEARS, a cloud-native platform for multi-lab FAIR data, but similarly serve as a proof of concept. Hao et al. (DOI: 10.51847/i178allztd) emphasize that a reusable experimental record must bind raw analytical traces to reagent identities, batch IDs, preparation history, environment, calibration state, software/model versions, branching decisions, manual interventions, and failures—metadata that current SDL records routinely omit (pqac-00000000). Steensen et al. confirm that ontologized data integration into optimization campaigns has not been achieved systematically (pqac-00000010).

## 3. Reproducibility and Round-Robin Benchmarking Between Labs

**Status: UNSOLVED.** No accepted multi-lab round-robin protocol for SDLs exists. Hao et al. call for prospective challenge sets involving noise, constraints, missing measurements, failed runs, distributional change, and long-duration campaigns that reveal instrument drift, reagent degradation, software changes, and maintenance burdens—none of which have been standardized (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000002, pqac-00000027). Silva et al. (DOI: 10.2172/3377973) highlight that LLM-based orchestration is nondeterministic, making run-to-run reproducibility difficult, and that verification infrastructure has not kept pace with agent capabilities; they recommend end-to-end reproduction benchmarks, uncertainty quantification, and full provenance recording of prompts, responses, decisions, data, tools, and model versions (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000030). Mallia and Caputo (DOI: 10.69709/caic.2026.133382) propose cross-platform transfer benchmarks and reference datasets for stress-testing candidate schemas, but note that poisoning-resistant model-exchange protocols and formal inter-lab protocols remain absent (pqac-00000024). Lee et al. call for reference experiments and calibration materials but do not describe established round-robin procedures (pqac-00000032).

## 4. Shortage of Negative Results

**Status: UNSOLVED.** Chemical datasets disproportionately retain successful outcomes. Gauthier et al. explicitly note that chemical datasets emphasize successes while omitting failed experiments, and their infrastructure is designed to capture both raw data and metadata for every experimental step including failures (pqac-00000012). Hao et al. emphasize that failed or negative experiments must be interpretable and systematically captured, distinguishing genuine null chemistry from analytical or robotic failure—an important distinction that current systems rarely make (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000004, pqac-00000006). The SDL community has not established incentive structures, data formats, or publication venues that routinely encourage sharing of negative autonomous-experiment outcomes, despite their importance for model training and avoiding selection bias.

## 5. Closing the Loop with Multiple Orthogonal Characterization Modalities

**Status: UNSOLVED.** Most operational SDLs optimize a single scalar objective (e.g., photoluminescence peak, conductivity, yield). Wakabayashi and Otsuka (DOI: 10.48550/arXiv.2608.26016) frame multimodal characterization—XRD, spectroscopy, microscopy, electrochemistry, process logs—as a major open problem requiring data fusion, uncertainty calibration, and decision models that can handle heterogeneous noise, cost, delay, scale, and missingness across modalities (pqac-00000040, pqac-00000041). Müller et al. (DOI: 10.48550/arXiv.2609.04564) demonstrate this concretely: a zero-yield result was ambiguous until the agent accessed raw NMR records, reconstructed the chemical-shift axis, and distinguished a real absence of product from an analytical failure—illustrating that scalar optimization collapses the evidence needed for diagnosis (pqac-00000016). Foadian et al. (DOI: 10.1021/acsmaterialsau.4c00096) emphasize that closing the characterization loop requires identifying rapid, reliable proxy signals that connect high-dimensional measurements to material compositions and functionalities (pqac-00000042). Hao et al. note that molecular plausibility, synthesis, assay activity, mechanism, cellular relevance, and stability are successive but non-equivalent evidence layers that a single scalar objective cannot represent (pqac-00000019).

## 6. Multi-Fidelity and Multi-Objective Optimization

**Status: UNSOLVED.** Wakabayashi and Otsuka provide the most detailed treatment, identifying that low-fidelity measurements are valuable only when sufficiently correlated with the high-fidelity target and inexpensive relative to the information they provide; weak correlation or systematic bias can waste the experimental budget (pqac-00000022). Acquisition functions must jointly balance expected improvement against source-specific costs and determine when further low-fidelity sampling is no longer worthwhile. For multi-objective campaigns, Pareto hypervolume methods become costly, scalarization can compress trade-offs, and batch methods must handle conflicting properties, feasibility constraints, and asynchronous execution (pqac-00000018, pqac-00000020). Hippalgaonkar et al. (DOI: 10.21203/rs.3.rs-3578558/v1) developed EGBO specifically to handle constrained multi-objective problems in SDLs, confirming that standard acquisition functions are insufficient. The battery domain adds long cycling times and substantial cell-to-cell variability, making exhaustive exploration impractical (pqac-00000044, pqac-00000046).

## 7. Transfer/Meta-Learning Across Chemistries

**Status: UNSOLVED.** Transfer is promising within closely related campaigns (e.g., across precursor batches for quantum-dot synthesis, yielding at least twofold acceleration) but unproven across genuinely different chemical systems (pqac-00000021, pqac-00000047). Wakabayashi and Otsuka warn that negative transfer is a realistic risk when source and target systems differ in descriptors, objectives, scales, or failure semantics (pqac-00000043, pqac-00000045). Experimental drift—source depletion, chamber evolution, catalyst aging, batch replacement, calibration changes—can make nominally comparable measurements non-transferable, requiring time-, state-, or change-point-aware surrogate models and reference experiments to assess whether historical data remain reusable (pqac-00000041). Mallia and Caputo identify the cold-start problem and platform specialization as fundamental barriers, proposing foundation models and transfer learning as solutions subject to data-poisoning risks (pqac-00000001). Bennett et al. (DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-74425-x) note that transfer learning and descriptor-based approaches represent future directions for their autonomous catalysis platform (pqac-00000017). Systematic meta-learning demonstrations across genuinely different chemistries remain scarce.

## 8. Human-in-the-Loop and Error Recovery

**Status: UNSOLVED.** Cheng et al. (DOI: 10.20944/preprints202608.0273.v1) provide the most detailed treatment, arguing that autonomous systems must handle silent execution failures, instrument drift, biological variability, sample mix-ups, incomplete troubleshooting, and discrepancies between protocol intent and actual execution (pqac-00000026, pqac-00000028). They call for continuous verification, observability, provenance logs, quality-control artifacts, anomaly feedback, recovery mechanisms, abstention, and escalation to human judgment. Hao et al. emphasize that platforms may lack the perception and adaptability required for unfamiliar samples and failure states, and that co-design must establish admissible actions, stopping rules, and escalation pathways before autonomous operation begins (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000027). Lee et al. note that SDL safety requires contextual hazard detection, predictive diagnostics, automatic recovery, safety-aware planning, and real-time mitigation for unattended operation—capabilities beyond simple threshold alarms (pqac-00000033). Silva et al. frame reliable human override, screening, auditing, and independent measurements as essential research concerns, noting that agents perform near or below chance on some reproducibility benchmarks (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000030).

## 9. Cost and Accessibility

**Status: UNSOLVED.** Cost remains a decisive barrier to broad adoption. Lo et al. (DOI: 10.1039/d3dd00223c) document the full range: from frugal-twin setups at ~$50–$450 (e.g., MIK-I at ~$450, Jubilee at ~$2,000) to research-grade platforms at $10,000–$30,000, up to industrial systems like the Maholo LabDroid at ~$890,000 (pqac-00000051, pqac-00000052, pqac-00000054, pqac-00000055, pqac-00000057). A benchtop NMR alone costs ~$40,000, and robust low-cost alternatives to NMR or HPLC-MS under $10,000 do not currently exist (pqac-00000054). Mallia and Caputo describe current SDLs as requiring multi-million-euro bespoke investments concentrated in elite institutions, and propose Laboratory-as-a-Service, cloud access, secure tele-operation, standardized experiment descriptions, metered pricing, and open-source hardware to broaden equitable access (pqac-00000024). Jiang et al. recommend decentralized resource-sharing, cloud simulation, and shared equipment hubs to reduce capital and operating costs for smaller institutions (pqac-00000005). Lo et al. emphasize that affordability is context-dependent: prices considered low-cost in developed countries may be unaffordable in the Global South due to limited funding, delivery expenses, and foreign-exchange difficulties (pqac-00000057). Multi-fidelity strategies—where inexpensive frugal-twin SDLs explore the parameter space before costly high-fidelity systems refine promising regions—are proposed as a practical cost-reduction mechanism (pqac-00000058).

## Conclusion: All Nine Challenges Remain Unsolved

Based on this survey of 15+ recent reviews, perspectives, and roadmap papers, **all nine named challenges remain open problems as of 2026**. None is described as fully resolved by any source consulted. Partial progress includes: SiLA2 and OPC UA gaining adoption as device-level protocols; Matryoshka files and SEARS as FAIR-data exemplars; EGBO and related algorithms for constrained multi-objective optimization; within-campaign transfer learning for nanocrystal synthesis; HeinSight 4.0 for vision-guided error detection; and frugal-twin systems for democratized prototyping and education. However, the gap between these individual advances and the integrated, interoperable, reproducible, accessible, and trustworthy SDL 2.0 envisioned by the community remains substantial.

It does, however, describe broader problems that such standards must address in self-driving laboratories. High-throughput experiments produce many files from heterogeneous instruments and platforms, making consistent interpretation, integration, and semantic interoperability difficult. Swiss Cat+ addresses these issues through a dedicated FAIR research data infrastructure (RDI), ontology-driven metadata modeling, standardized ASM-JSON analytical outputs, and automated workflow orchestration using Kubernetes and Argo. Its pipeline handles nested “Matryoshka” archives, extracts and normalizes metadata, converts JSON-derived content into RDF/Turtle, validates the resulting data with SHACL, and exposes it through a SPARQL endpoint and user interface. A feedback loop corrects and reprocesses data that fail validation. The infrastructure is intended to support reproducibility, machine-actionable data, semantic search, scalability, and AI readiness. These details are relevant to interoperability between laboratory platforms because they emphasize common vocabularies, formal schemas, validation, linked data, and separation between internal storage, workflow services, RDF databases, and user-facing tools. Interoperability is essential because different laboratory workflows and database platforms must exchange data seamlessly and support machine-learning or other downstream tools. Distributed research additionally requires cloud infrastructure and electronic lab notebooks that multiple laboratories can access and update concurrently. The excerpt presents SEARS as addressing these infrastructure-level needs through provenance-rich capture, immutable audit trails, ontology-driven data entry, arbitrary-file storage with JSON sidecars, versioning, REST APIs, and a Python SDK. These capabilities are positioned as complementary enabling infrastructure for multi-lab orchestration, not as a replacement for scientific methods or a direct comparison of orchestration standards.

Multi-fidelity optimization must balance cheap, fast, imperfect measurements against expensive, accurate evaluations and decide when low-fidelity information is sufficiently informative to justify high-fidelity experiments; the excerpt does not yet detail the associated model assumptions or transferability challenges. The passage also does not specifically discuss transfer learning or meta-learning across chemical systems. It does suggest that rich, heterogeneous modalities—spectra, AFM and microscopy images, and process logs—could be converted into learned representations before GP-based decision-making. However, deep representations introduce additional parameters and require informative data, reliable pretraining, and validation against simpler baselines. Thus, closing the loop over multiple orthogonal modalities rather than a scalar objective remains dependent on reliable fusion, uncertainty calibration, and decision models, issues not fully resolved here.

contexts.context: The excerpt establishes the core architecture and several defining directions of SDL 2.0. A self-driving laboratory combines automated hardware, AI, and data infrastructure; its performance depends on coordinated experimental throughput, information management, and intelligent decision-making. SDL 2.0 is characterized by flexible discovery across chemical reactions, materials systems, and experimental modalities with minimal reconfiguration, supported by modular hardware, interoperable systems, computer vision, large language models, and orchestration software. Orchestration must schedule experiments, manage data, coordinate robotic trajectories and parallel tasks, and reduce idle time. Interoperability and standardized communication are essential for generalization and reliable distributed systems. Data must be systematically collected, standardized, and managed according to FAIR principles so multimodal AI can reduce noise and extract features. AI methods such as Bayesian optimization, reinforcement learning, and foundation models create iterative self-improving feedback loops. The excerpt also contrasts compact unit-based systems with station-based distributed systems: the former are easier to control and replace but less scalable, while the latter are more flexible and scalable but demand sophisticated coordination, protocols, and robotic control. contexts.context: This excerpt addresses several themes relevant to SDL 2.0, but it does not provide the complete list of six defining characteristics or the full discussion of open problems involving interoperability, safety, creativity, generalizability, negative results, and round-robin benchmarking. It emphasizes parallelization as a means of increasing throughput and reducing experimental time, while noting the trade-off between parallel decision-making and the number of trials. Networks of identical low-cost SDLs can allow geographically distant laboratories to build clones, compare variability across robot instances, and conduct high-throughput materials-discovery campaigns. Asynchronous optimization improves resource use when experiment runtimes vary by launching new experiments as equipment becomes available, although redundant or low-value suggestions must be avoided. Multi-fidelity optimization combines inexpensive, lower-accuracy SDLs with costly, higher-fidelity systems to reduce overall optimization cost while preserving accuracy. The excerpt also identifies workflow orchestration as important for multistep experiments. Cloud laboratories may improve academic access and promote open science, but require substantial capital, technical expertise, security, queuing, access-control, and orchestration infrastructure; human technicians may still be needed for sample transfer. These requirements can make cloud access prohibitive for educational and citizen-science users, whereas low-cost SDLs offer smaller scale and lower data-security risks.

Interoperability remains difficult because hardware-specific communication protocols, the absence of shared digital infrastructures, standardized automation architectures, common interfaces, calibration benchmarks, and machine-readable data formats impede reproducibility, scalability, and multi-laboratory campaigns. Creativity through generative AI is constrained by models lacking chemical knowledge, interpretability, and experimental feasibility, while human translation of AI proposals into executable protocols remains a bottleneck. Collaboration also requires better interfaces and structured human feedback so scientists can guide autonomous campaigns. Safe SDLs should combine multimodal hazard detection with autonomous recovery rather than merely stopping experiments. They should monitor vision, gases, acoustics, thermal behavior, and equipment signals; detect abnormal trends; perform interventions such as spill cleanup or reaction quenching; support predictive maintenance; and prevent unsafe sequences through scheduler-level safety logic. SDL 2.0 is envisioned as a transition from narrow, first-generation closed-loop systems toward flexible, scalable, globally networked platforms. Generalizability addresses SDL 1.0’s narrow scope and dependence on handcrafted features or human-curated heuristics. Collaboration is enabled through community-driven standards, cloud connectivity, and globally distributed experimentation. Safety and creativity are presented as core design goals, with AI supporting reasoning, hypothesis generation, and discovery of unexpected phenomena. The review anticipates integration of synthesis, characterization, and theory, while emphasizing reproducibility, accelerated innovation, democratized access, and human–AI collaboration. XRD, spectroscopy, microscopy, electrical or electrochemical measurements, and process histories are heterogeneous data sources that are not necessarily available for every sample. The excerpt therefore points toward time-, state-, or change-point-aware surrogate models and reference experiments to assess whether historical data remain reusable. It does not give detailed prescriptions for multi-fidelity Bayesian optimization, but its discussion implies challenges from unequal measurement availability, changing reliability, and non-comparable data across systems.

Transfer learning is not reliably beneficial: information from one source task may accelerate optimization, while another seemingly related modality can cause negative transfer. contexts.context: The excerpt frames loop closure across multiple characterization methods as substantially more difficult than optimizing a single scalar objective. The principal challenge is identifying rapid, reliable proxy signals that can connect high-dimensional measurements to the material compositions and functionalities relevant to real-world use. Closing the characterization loop requires integrating complementary methods so that their combined data provide a comprehensive picture, rather than reducing each experiment to one isolated score. This creates difficulties in data integration, interpretation, and experimental decision-making, particularly as the workflow moves from rapid discovery toward scalable manufacturing, where consistency, reliability, and validation become essential. The excerpt also emphasizes that navigating broad composition and processing spaces requires coupling theory and experiment. Machine-learning models are effective at interpolation within known data but become uncertain when asked to extrapolate to new compositions, conditions, molecules, or processing parameters. Thus, multi-fidelity optimization and transfer across chemical systems would face the general problem of inadequate coverage and mismatch between the training data and the target space; the supplied passage does not provide specific methods or results for multi-fidelity Bayesian optimization or transfer learning. Human expertise, hypothesis generation, and domain knowledge are presented as necessary complements to ML for selecting promising unexplored regions and refining predictions.

contexts.context: The excerpt identifies several cost and accessibility challenges for self-driving laboratories (SDLs). SDLs combine sophisticated science, hardware, and software, making them complex and expensive to build. Researchers may face a “jack of all trades, master of none” trade-off, sacrificing scientific capability, hardware quality, or software development, or requiring large multidisciplinary teams. High-cost instruments also create barriers: a benchtop NMR is described as costing $40,000, while robust low-cost alternatives to NMR or HPLC-MS under $10,000 are not currently available. SDLs can additionally impose a substantial training burden, and mistakes may be costly. The frugal twin is presented as a lower-cost, relaxed-requirement version of an SDL that trades some accuracy or capability for affordability, rapid prototyping, and lower-risk experimentation. It allows researchers and students to test hardware, software, scientific objectives, and optimization algorithms iteratively before deploying them on expensive systems. contexts.context: The excerpt identifies high acquisition and operating costs as a major accessibility barrier for self-driving laboratories (SDLs), especially because advanced analytical instruments such as NMR and HPLC-MS can cost hundreds of thousands of dollars. Cost reduction generally requires either scaling back research capabilities or accepting lower accuracy and precision, creating trade-offs in usefulness. Some high-cost capabilities may not have practical low-cost substitutes: for example, inexpensive infrared monitoring can support low-fidelity reaction monitoring but cannot replace NMR or HPLC-MS for unknown-compound characterization. The “frugal twin” is a low-cost counterpart of a high-cost SDL, positioned along a spectrum trading cost against research capability. It can provide a low-risk setting for rapid prototyping, education, and transferable skills, while generating preliminary evidence or feasibility results that may support later investment in a more capable SDL. The excerpt gives a concrete setup cost of approximately $450 for MIK-I, a frugal twin of a more advanced automated synthesis system. Other examples range from simple dye-mixing and LEGO-based liquid-handling systems to more capable platforms, but no additional specific dollar or euro prices are stated in this excerpt. The concept therefore addresses democratization by making automation accessible for institutions, researchers, and students with limited resources, even when full high-end SDL functionality remains unavailable.

contexts.context: The excerpt emphasizes that SDL affordability is highly context-dependent. A price considered low-cost by a research group in a developed country may be unaffordable for a school or laboratory in a developing country because of limited funding, delivery expenses, unfair pricing, foreign-exchange difficulties, and competing livelihood priorities. Grant and institutional purchasing rules also affect accessibility: the review notes a 5000 USD threshold for distinguishing consumables from equipment and gives the Opentrons OT-2 as an example at approximately 7500 USD, potentially requiring dedicated support. The table demonstrates a broad range of low-cost SDL setups, including educational and research platforms costing about 50, 200, 250, 300, 416, 450, 500, 600, 650, 830, 934, 1000, 2000, 2050, 3000, 4160, 5000, 10,000, 15,000, and 30,000 USD. Examples include low-cost spectroscopy and Bayesian-optimization systems, titration platforms, MOF and nanomaterial synthesis systems, and “The Chemputer.” The frugal twin is introduced as a low-cost counterpart to a physical entity, inspired by the digital-twin concept. Its purpose is to preserve core real-world system principles at an education-friendly cost, using modularity, hardware reuse, high-throughput approaches, and cloud experimentation to reduce complexity and barriers to entry, thereby supporting broader democratization of SDLs.

contexts.context: The excerpt identifies several cost and accessibility challenges for self-driving laboratories (SDLs). Parallelization can improve throughput, but it requires purchasing additional hardware and involves a trade-off between speed and the total number of trials. High-fidelity instruments and reproducible experimental setups are expensive, motivating multi-fidelity strategies in which inexpensive, lower-fidelity SDLs explore the parameter space before costly, higher-fidelity systems refine promising regions. Cloud laboratories can reduce barriers for academics, but they require substantial capital and specialized expertise for onboarding, security, access controls, queuing, workflow orchestration, and sample transfer; these infrastructure expenses are passed to users and may be prohibitive for education and citizen science. The frugal twin concept is represented by building low-cost SDLs that reproduce or complement more expensive systems. Such systems can be cloned across geographically distant laboratories, enabling networks of parallel robots and broader access to advanced research capabilities. The excerpt explicitly states that the SDL hardware components in the discussed example cost “#500 USD” (apparently indicating approximately $500 USD). No euro-denominated setup cost is specified in this excerpt. The passage also mentions CMU Cloud Lab as an institutional approach to lowering access barriers and promoting open science.

answer.formatted_answer:
Question: What do recent (2023-2026) reviews, perspectives and roadmap papers identify as the OPEN PROBLEMS and FUTURE DIRECTIONS for self-driving laboratories, specifically in materials chemistry and electrochemistry? Give DOIs. I want the concrete, named challenges rather than generalities: orchestration/interoperability standards (SiLA2, LabOP, AnIML, Bluesky, Chemputer/chi), FAIR data and metadata capture, reproducibility and round-robin benchmarking between labs, the shortage of negative results, closing the loop with multiple ORTHOGONAL characterization modalities rather than a single scalar objective, multi-fidelity and multi-objective optimization, transfer/meta-learning across chemistries, human-in-the-loop and error recovery, and cost/accessibility. Which of these are described as still unsolved as of 2026?

# Open Problems and Future Directions for Self-Driving Laboratories in Materials Chemistry and Electrochemistry (2023–2026)

## Overview

A systematic survey of recent reviews, perspectives, and roadmap papers (2023–2026) reveals a clear consensus: while self-driving laboratories (SDLs) have demonstrated impressive domain-specific capabilities—from nanoparticle synthesis to electrocatalyst screening—the transition from narrow, single-loop demonstrations to general-purpose, networked, trustworthy autonomous discovery platforms remains incomplete. The SDL 2.0 vision articulated by Lee et al. (DOI: 10.1039/d5mh01984b) defines six pillars—interoperability, collaboration, generalizability, orchestration, safety, and creativity—all of which remain aspirational rather than realized (lee2026towardselfdrivinglaboratory pages 17-19, lee2026towardselfdrivinglaboratory pages 1-2). The comprehensive Chemical Reviews survey by Tom et al. (DOI: 10.1021/acs.chemrev.4c00055) and the Trustworthy Autonomous Science roadmap by Silva et al. (DOI: 10.2172/3377973) further confirm that the field has not yet achieved end-to-end, experimentally self-validating autonomous discovery (silva2026towardtrustworthyautonomous pages 6-9, tom2024selfdrivinglaboratoriesfor pages 7-8, tom2024selfdrivinglaboratoriesfor pages 56-57).

All nine remain unsolved, although several have partial standards, prototype infrastructures, or domain-specific demonstrations.*

## 1. Orchestration and Interoperability Standards (SiLA2, LabOP, AnIML, Bluesky, Chemputer/XDL)

**Status: UNSOLVED.** No universally adopted standard spans instruments, workflow descriptions, analytical formats, and orchestration layers. Tom et al. identify the absence of standardized APIs from instrument manufacturers as a fundamental bottleneck, presenting SiLA2 as a promising device-communication protocol modeled on ROS but requiring much broader adoption (tom2024selfdrivinglaboratoriesfor pages 7-8). Lee et al. recommend SiLA and OPC UA for standardized interfaces alongside modular, open-source orchestration software, while acknowledging that hardware-specific communication protocols, absence of shared digital infrastructure, and lack of common calibration benchmarks continue to impede scalability and reproducibility (lee2026towardselfdrivinglaboratory pages 17-19, lee2026towardselfdrivinglaboratory pages 20-21). Steensen et al. (DOI: 10.1002/aidi.202500067) document that materials-science ontologies remain immature and that semantic data integration has in practice been post hoc rather than built into live campaigns (steensen2026thenecessityof pages 3-3, steensen2026thenecessityof pages 2-3). Jiang et al. (DOI: 10.4208/cicc.2025.90.03) specifically call for universal communication protocols such as SiLA2 and AnIML to standardize cross-platform compatibility (jiang2025recentprogressin pages 11-12). Critically, syntactic portability of a protocol file does not guarantee chemically equivalent execution across heterogeneous platforms—a point emphasized as a fundamental reproducibility risk (hao2026doselfdrivinglaboratories pages 4-5).

## 2. FAIR Data and Metadata Capture

**Status: UNSOLVED.** Data remain fragmented across bespoke instrument-specific files and laboratory-specific schemas. Gauthier et al. (DOI: 10.1039/d5dd00297d) demonstrate a FAIR research data infrastructure for the Swiss Cat+ platform using Matryoshka files, ontology-driven metadata modeling, ASM-JSON analytical outputs, RDF/Turtle conversion, and SHACL validation—but this remains a single-site exemplar rather than a community standard (gauthier2025afairresearch pages 3-5, gauthier2025afairresearch pages 1-2, gauthier2025afairresearch pages 2-3). Tali et al. (DOI: 10.1039/d5dd00175g) present SEARS, a cloud-native platform for multi-lab FAIR data, but similarly serve as a proof of concept. Hao et al. (DOI: 10.51847/i178allztd) emphasize that a reusable experimental record must bind raw analytical traces to reagent identities, batch IDs, preparation history, environment, calibration state, software/model versions, branching decisions, manual interventions, and failures—metadata that current SDL records routinely omit (hao2026doselfdrivinglaboratories pages 6-8). Steensen et al. confirm that ontologized data integration into optimization campaigns has not been achieved systematically (steensen2026thenecessityof pages 3-3).

## 3. Reproducibility and Round-Robin Benchmarking Between Labs

**Status: UNSOLVED.** No accepted multi-lab round-robin protocol for SDLs exists. Hao et al. call for prospective challenge sets involving noise, constraints, missing measurements, failed runs, distributional change, and long-duration campaigns that reveal instrument drift, reagent degradation, software changes, and maintenance burdens—none of which have been standardized (hao2026doselfdrivinglaboratories pages 6-8, hao2026doselfdrivinglaboratories pages 8-10, hao2026doselfdrivinglaboratories pages 8-8). Silva et al. (DOI: 10.2172/3377973) highlight that LLM-based orchestration is nondeterministic, making run-to-run reproducibility difficult, and that verification infrastructure has not kept pace with agent capabilities; they recommend end-to-end reproduction benchmarks, uncertainty quantification, and full provenance recording of prompts, responses, decisions, data, tools, and model versions (silva2026towardtrustworthyautonomous pages 17-18, silva2026towardtrustworthyautonomous pages 15-17). Mallia and Caputo (DOI: 10.69709/caic.2026.133382) propose cross-platform transfer benchmarks and reference datasets for stress-testing candidate schemas, but note that poisoning-resistant model-exchange protocols and formal inter-lab protocols remain absent (mallia2026aiguidedselfdrivinglaboratories pages 22-27). Lee et al. call for reference experiments and calibration materials but do not describe established round-robin procedures (lee2026towardselfdrivinglaboratory pages 19-20).

## 4. Shortage of Negative Results

**Status: UNSOLVED.** Chemical datasets disproportionately retain successful outcomes. Gauthier et al. explicitly note that chemical datasets emphasize successes while omitting failed experiments, and their infrastructure is designed to capture both raw data and metadata for every experimental step including failures (gauthier2025afairresearch pages 1-2). Hao et al. emphasize that failed or negative experiments must be interpretable and systematically captured, distinguishing genuine null chemistry from analytical or robotic failure—an important distinction that current systems rarely make (hao2026doselfdrivinglaboratories pages 6-8, hao2026doselfdrivinglaboratories pages 8-8, hao2026doselfdrivinglaboratories pages 4-5). The SDL community has not established incentive structures, data formats, or publication venues that routinely encourage sharing of negative autonomous-experiment outcomes, despite their importance for model training and avoiding selection bias.

## 5. Closing the Loop with Multiple Orthogonal Characterization Modalities

**Status: UNSOLVED.** Most operational SDLs optimize a single scalar objective (e.g., photoluminescence peak, conductivity, yield). Wakabayashi and Otsuka (DOI: 10.48550/arXiv.2608.26016) frame multimodal characterization—XRD, spectroscopy, microscopy, electrochemistry, process logs—as a major open problem requiring data fusion, uncertainty calibration, and decision models that can handle heterogeneous noise, cost, delay, scale, and missingness across modalities (wakabayashi2608bayesianoptimizationfor pages 1-3, wakabayashi2608bayesianoptimizationfor pages 45-48). Müller et al. (DOI: 10.48550/arXiv.2609.04564) demonstrate this concretely: a zero-yield result was ambiguous until the agent accessed raw NMR records, reconstructed the chemical-shift axis, and distinguished a real absence of product from an analytical failure—illustrating that scalar optimization collapses the evidence needed for diagnosis (muller2026laagente\optimatowards pages 11-13). Foadian et al. (DOI: 10.1021/acsmaterialsau.4c00096) emphasize that closing the characterization loop requires identifying rapid, reliable proxy signals that connect high-dimensional measurements to material compositions and functionalities (foadian2024fromsunlightto pages 8-9). Hao et al. note that molecular plausibility, synthesis, assay activity, mechanism, cellular relevance, and stability are successive but non-equivalent evidence layers that a single scalar objective cannot represent (hao2026doselfdrivinglaboratories pages 8-8).

## 6. Multi-Fidelity and Multi-Objective Optimization

**Status: UNSOLVED.** Wakabayashi and Otsuka provide the most detailed treatment, identifying that low-fidelity measurements are valuable only when sufficiently correlated with the high-fidelity target and inexpensive relative to the information they provide; weak correlation or systematic bias can waste the experimental budget (wakabayashi2608bayesianoptimizationfor pages 26-28). Acquisition functions must jointly balance expected improvement against source-specific costs and determine when further low-fidelity sampling is no longer worthwhile. For multi-objective campaigns, Pareto hypervolume methods become costly, scalarization can compress trade-offs, and batch methods must handle conflicting properties, feasibility constraints, and asynchronous execution (wakabayashi2608bayesianoptimizationfor pages 16-17, wakabayashi2608bayesianoptimizationfor pages 1-3). Hippalgaonkar et al. (DOI: 10.21203/rs.3.rs-3578558/v1) developed EGBO specifically to handle constrained multi-objective problems in SDLs, confirming that standard acquisition functions are insufficient. The battery domain adds long cycling times and substantial cell-to-cell variability, making exhaustive exploration impractical (wakabayashi2608bayesianoptimizationfor pages 40-42, wakabayashi2608bayesianoptimizationfor pages 42-44).

## 7. Transfer/Meta-Learning Across Chemistries

**Status: UNSOLVED.** Transfer is promising within closely related campaigns (e.g., across precursor batches for quantum-dot synthesis, yielding at least twofold acceleration) but unproven across genuinely different chemical systems (hao2025autonomousmaterialssynthesis pages 53-56). Wakabayashi and Otsuka warn that negative transfer is a realistic risk when source and target systems differ in descriptors, objectives, scales, or failure semantics (wakabayashi2608bayesianoptimizationfor pages 33-36, wakabayashi2608bayesianoptimizationfor pages 31-33). Experimental drift—source depletion, chamber evolution, catalyst aging, batch replacement, calibration changes—can make nominally comparable measurements non-transferable, requiring time-, state-, or change-point-aware surrogate models and reference experiments to assess whether historical data remain reusable (wakabayashi2608bayesianoptimizationfor pages 45-48). Mallia and Caputo identify the cold-start problem and platform specialization as fundamental barriers, proposing foundation models and transfer learning as solutions subject to data-poisoning risks (mallia2026aiguidedselfdrivinglaboratories pages 17-22). Bennett et al. (DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-74425-x) note that transfer learning and descriptor-based approaches represent future directions for their autonomous catalysis platform (muller2026laagente\optimatowards pages 9-11). Systematic meta-learning demonstrations across genuinely different chemistries remain scarce.

## 8. Human-in-the-Loop and Error Recovery

**Status: UNSOLVED.** Cheng et al. (DOI: 10.20944/preprints202608.0273.v1) provide the most detailed treatment, arguing that autonomous systems must handle silent execution failures, instrument drift, biological variability, sample mix-ups, incomplete troubleshooting, and discrepancies between protocol intent and actual execution (cheng2026towardshumanledagentdriven pages 7-8, cheng2026towardshumanledagentdriven pages 8-11). They call for continuous verification, observability, provenance logs, quality-control artifacts, anomaly feedback, recovery mechanisms, abstention, and escalation to human judgment. Hao et al. emphasize that platforms may lack the perception and adaptability required for unfamiliar samples and failure states, and that co-design must establish admissible actions, stopping rules, and escalation pathways before autonomous operation begins (hao2026doselfdrivinglaboratories pages 6-8, hao2026doselfdrivinglaboratories pages 8-8). Lee et al. note that SDL safety requires contextual hazard detection, predictive diagnostics, automatic recovery, safety-aware planning, and real-time mitigation for unattended operation—capabilities beyond simple threshold alarms (lee2026towardselfdrivinglaboratory pages 17-19). Silva et al. frame reliable human override, screening, auditing, and independent measurements as essential research concerns, noting that agents perform near or below chance on some reproducibility benchmarks (silva2026towardtrustworthyautonomous pages 17-18, silva2026towardtrustworthyautonomous pages 15-17).

## 9. Cost and Accessibility

**Status: UNSOLVED.** Cost remains a decisive barrier to broad adoption. Lo et al. (DOI: 10.1039/d3dd00223c) document the full range: from frugal-twin setups at ~$50–$450 (e.g., MIK-I at ~$450, Jubilee at ~$2,000) to research-grade platforms at $10,000–$30,000, up to industrial systems like the Maholo LabDroid at ~$890,000 (lo2024reviewoflowcost pages 22-23, lo2024reviewoflowcost pages 5-6, lo2024reviewoflowcost pages 6-7, lo2024reviewoflowcost pages 10-11, lo2024reviewoflowcost pages 4-5). A benchtop NMR alone costs ~$40,000, and robust low-cost alternatives to NMR or HPLC-MS under $10,000 do not currently exist (lo2024reviewoflowcost pages 6-7). Mallia and Caputo describe current SDLs as requiring multi-million-euro bespoke investments concentrated in elite institutions, and propose Laboratory-as-a-Service, cloud access, secure tele-operation, standardized experiment descriptions, metered pricing, and open-source hardware to broaden equitable access (mallia2026aiguidedselfdrivinglaboratories pages 22-27). Jiang et al. recommend decentralized resource-sharing, cloud simulation, and shared equipment hubs to reduce capital and operating costs for smaller institutions (jiang2025recentprogressin pages 11-12). Lo et al. emphasize that affordability is context-dependent: prices considered low-cost in developed countries may be unaffordable in the Global South due to limited funding, delivery expenses, and foreign-exchange difficulties (lo2024reviewoflowcost pages 4-5). Multi-fidelity strategies—where inexpensive frugal-twin SDLs explore the parameter space before costly high-fidelity systems refine promising regions—are proposed as a practical cost-reduction mechanism (lo2024reviewoflowcost pages 17-18).

## Conclusion: All Nine Challenges Remain Unsolved

Based on this survey of 15+ recent reviews, perspectives, and roadmap papers, **all nine named challenges remain open problems as of 2026**. None is described as fully resolved by any source consulted. Partial progress includes: SiLA2 and OPC UA gaining adoption as device-level protocols; Matryoshka files and SEARS as FAIR-data exemplars; EGBO and related algorithms for constrained multi-objective optimization; within-campaign transfer learning for nanocrystal synthesis; HeinSight 4.0 for vision-guided error detection; and frugal-twin systems for democratized prototyping and education. However, the gap between these individual advances and the integrated, interoperable, reproducible, accessible, and trustworthy SDL 2.0 envisioned by the community remains substantial.

| Challenge | Status as of 2026 | Concrete unresolved issues identified in the literature | Key references and DOIs |
|---|---|---|---|
| Orchestration/interoperability standards (SiLA2, LabOP, AnIML, Bluesky, Chemputer/chi) | **UNSOLVED — partial, fragmented progress** | No universally adopted interface spans instruments, workflow descriptions, analytical formats, and orchestration layers. Vendor instruments often lack standardized APIs; static task graphs cannot reliably branch, resume, reallocate resources, or respond to drift; materials ontologies remain immature and weakly adopted. SiLA2/SiLA and OPC UA are promising device interfaces, AnIML addresses analytical data, LabOP and Chemputer/XDL represent procedures, and Bluesky provides acquisition orchestration—but the literature does **not** establish end-to-end interoperability among them or with `chi`. Syntactic portability also does not guarantee chemically equivalent execution across platforms. (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000014, pqac-00000033, pqac-00000037) | Tom et al., [10.1021/acs.chemrev.4c00055](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.chemrev.4c00055); Lee et al., [10.1039/d5mh01984b](https://doi.org/10.1039/d5mh01984b); Steensen et al., [10.1002/aidi.202500067](https://doi.org/10.1002/aidi.202500067); Jiang et al., [10.4208/cicc.2025.90.03](https://doi.org/10.4208/cicc.2025.90.03) |
| FAIR data and metadata capture | **UNSOLVED — working exemplars exist, not community-wide infrastructure** | Data remain fragmented across bespoke instrument files and laboratory schemas. A reusable record must bind raw traces to reagents and batch IDs, preparation history, environment, calibration and instrument state, software/model versions, preprocessing, branching decisions, manual interventions, failures, and uncertainty. Matryoshka files, semantic RDF/SHACL pipelines, SEARS, ontologies, and knowledge graphs demonstrate possible implementations, but ontology adoption and integration into live campaigns remain limited; some semantic conversion is still post hoc. (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000010, pqac-00000012, pqac-00000015) | Gauthier et al., [10.1039/d5dd00297d](https://doi.org/10.1039/d5dd00297d); Tali et al., [10.1039/d5dd00175g](https://doi.org/10.1039/d5dd00175g); Hao et al., [10.51847/i178allztd](https://doi.org/10.51847/i178allztd); Steensen et al., [10.1002/aidi.202500067](https://doi.org/10.1002/aidi.202500067) |
| Reproducibility and round-robin benchmarking between labs | **UNSOLVED — requirements proposed; accepted round-robin regime absent** | The field lacks standard multi-lab challenge sets and formal round-robin protocols that test the same recipes, samples, calibrants, and decision policies across heterogeneous platforms. Needed tests include prospective and independent replication, protocol-equivalence checks, orthogonal confirmation, long-duration campaigns, drift and missing-data stress tests, failed runs, distribution shifts, and comparisons with human-directed workflows. Agent/LLM nondeterminism adds a requirement to preserve prompts, plans, tool calls, approvals, environments, model/data versions, uncertainty, and recovery traces—not merely final outputs. (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000024, pqac-00000025, pqac-00000027, pqac-00000030) | Hao et al., [10.51847/i178allztd](https://doi.org/10.51847/i178allztd); Silva et al., [10.2172/3377973](https://doi.org/10.2172/3377973); Mallia and Caputo, [10.69709/caic.2026.133382](https://doi.org/10.69709/caic.2026.133382); Lee et al., [10.1039/d5mh01984b](https://doi.org/10.1039/d5mh01984b) |
| Shortage of negative results | **UNSOLVED — technically capturable, culturally and infrastructurally underreported** | Chemical datasets disproportionately retain successful outcomes, while failed synthesis, null measurements, infeasible regions, aborted runs, and troubleshooting decisions are omitted or collapsed into ambiguous zeros. This biases models and acquisition policies and prevents systems from distinguishing bad chemistry from analytical or robotic failure. Future records must preserve interpretable negative outcomes with raw evidence, failure taxonomy, provenance, and recovery actions. (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000004, pqac-00000006, pqac-00000012, pqac-00000015) | Gauthier et al., [10.1039/d5dd00297d](https://doi.org/10.1039/d5dd00297d); Hao et al., [10.51847/i178allztd](https://doi.org/10.51847/i178allztd) |
| Closing the loop with multiple ORTHOGONAL characterization modalities rather than a single scalar objective | **UNSOLVED — isolated multimodal demonstrations, no general fusion-and-decision framework** | XRD, spectroscopy, microscopy, electrochemistry, imaging, process logs, and device tests observe different material states and arrive with different noise, cost, delay, scale, and missingness. SDLs must link every derived objective to raw signals and quality controls, diagnose modality-specific failure, reconcile conflicting evidence, and choose whether the next action should optimize performance, reduce uncertainty, repeat a measurement, or invoke another modality. Reducing all evidence to one scalar can hide phase purity, degradation, mechanism, stability, or analytical failure. (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000018, pqac-00000040, pqac-00000041, pqac-00000042) | Wakabayashi and Otsuka, [10.48550/arXiv.2608.26016](https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2608.26016); Foadian et al., [10.1021/acsmaterialsau.4c00096](https://doi.org/10.1021/acsmaterialsau.4c00096); Müller et al., [10.48550/arXiv.2609.04564](https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2609.04564); Hao et al., [10.51847/i178allztd](https://doi.org/10.51847/i178allztd) |
| Multi-fidelity and multi-objective optimization | **UNSOLVED — algorithms exist, robust laboratory deployment remains problem-specific** | Multi-fidelity planners must learn source-specific bias and correlation and decide when a cheap simulation, proxy assay, or short electrochemical test is informative enough to defer an expensive synthesis, microscopy session, or long-duration cycling test. Weakly correlated fidelities can waste budget. Multi-objective campaigns must handle conflicting properties, feasibility and safety constraints, noisy outputs, asynchronous batches, replicates, and changing objectives. Scalarization can erase Pareto trade-offs; hypervolume methods become costly and sensitive to modeling assumptions. (pqac-00000018, pqac-00000020, pqac-00000021, pqac-00000022, pqac-00000046) | Wakabayashi and Otsuka, [10.48550/arXiv.2608.26016](https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2608.26016); Hippalgaonkar et al., [10.21203/rs.3.rs-3578558/v1](https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-3578558/v1); Lo et al., [10.1039/d3dd00223c](https://doi.org/10.1039/d3dd00223c) |
| Transfer/meta-learning across chemistries | **UNSOLVED — promising within related campaigns; cross-chemistry generalization unproven** | Warm starts require compatible descriptors, objectives, scales, constraints, and failure semantics. Changes in precursor lots, instruments, calibration, substrate, chamber history, catalyst aging, processing, or mechanism create distribution shift and negative-transfer risk. Source information therefore needs task/context labels, reference experiments, uncertainty-aware weighting, comparison against target-only baselines, and rejection when it ceases to help. Systematic meta-learning demonstrations across genuinely different chemistries remain scarce. (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000020, pqac-00000041, pqac-00000043, pqac-00000045) | Wakabayashi and Otsuka, [10.48550/arXiv.2608.26016](https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2608.26016); Mallia and Caputo, [10.69709/caic.2026.133382](https://doi.org/10.69709/caic.2026.133382); Bennett et al., [10.1038/s41467-026-74425-x](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-74425-x) |
| Human-in-the-loop and error recovery | **UNSOLVED — human supervision is still a requirement, not an optional fallback** | Unattended campaigns face silent analytical failures, sample mix-ups, sensor drift, reagent degradation, clogs, mechanical faults, unsafe proposals, and ambiguous protocol intent. Future systems need observability, identity checks, anomaly attribution, abstention, safe abortion, checkpoint/restart, self-calibration, automatic recovery, regression testing after updates, and standardized escalation/override rules. Humans must retain control of goals, constraints, stopping rules, high-consequence decisions, and interpretation; LLM/agent reasoning requires audit trails and guardrails. (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000026, pqac-00000028, pqac-00000029, pqac-00000033) | Cheng et al., [10.20944/preprints202608.0273.v1](https://doi.org/10.20944/preprints202608.0273.v1); Hao et al., [10.51847/i178allztd](https://doi.org/10.51847/i178allztd); Lee et al., [10.1039/d5mh01984b](https://doi.org/10.1039/d5mh01984b); Silva et al., [10.2172/3377973](https://doi.org/10.2172/3377973) |
| Cost/accessibility | **UNSOLVED — low-cost substitutes broaden training and prototyping but do not reproduce full capability** | Bespoke SDLs and high-end NMR, HPLC-MS, microscopy, and robotics remain concentrated in wealthy institutions; maintenance, integration expertise, consumables, security, scheduling, and onboarding add recurring costs. Reported contrasts include an approximately $890,000 LabDroid, approximately $40,000 benchtop NMR, and frugal systems from hundreds to tens of thousands of dollars. “Frugal twins,” open hardware, modular components, shared hubs, and cloud Laboratory-as-a-Service lower entry barriers, but sacrifice fidelity or scope and cloud infrastructure costs are passed to users; geographic and institutional inequity persists. (pqac-00000024, pqac-00000051, pqac-00000052, pqac-00000054, pqac-00000057, pqac-00000058) | Lo et al., [10.1039/d3dd00223c](https://doi.org/10.1039/d3dd00223c); Mallia and Caputo, [10.69709/caic.2026.133382](https://doi.org/10.69709/caic.2026.133382); Jiang et al., [10.4208/cicc.2025.90.03](https://doi.org/10.4208/cicc.2025.90.03) |

info.query: What do recent (2023-2026) reviews, perspectives and roadmap papers identify as the OPEN PROBLEMS and FUTURE DIRECTIONS for self-driving laboratories, specifically in materials chemistry and electrochemistry? Give DOIs. I want the concrete, named challenges rather than generalities: orchestration/interoperability standards (SiLA2, LabOP, AnIML, Bluesky, Chemputer/chi), FAIR data and metadata capture, reproducibility and round-robin benchmarking between labs, the shortage of negative results, closing the loop with multiple ORTHOGONAL characterization modalities rather than a single scalar objective, multi-fidelity and multi-objective optimization, transfer/meta-learning across chemistries, human-in-the-loop and error recovery, and cost/accessibility. Which of these are described as still unsolved as of 2026?
